title: Course tools and Python foundations
text:
This notebook introduces the small set of Python tools used throughout the course. It is not a comprehensive Python tutorial: the goal is to be comfortable loading, inspecting, selecting, filtering, and plotting engineering data.
Learning objectives

title: Course tools and Python foundations
text:
1. Import the Python libraries
The next cell demonstrates how to import a Python library.
import numpy as np makes the NumPy library available in this notebook. The as keyword assigns the short alias np to NumPy’s namespace, so we can write np.array(...) instead of the longer numpy.array(...). Using np is a common convention in scientific Python.

# Import NumPy first: it is the numerical-array tool used in this section.
import numpy as np

title: Course tools and Python foundations
text:
2. Numerical arrays
A NumPy array stores a collection of numerical values. Array operations act element-by-element, which makes calculations compact and readable.

# Store repeated temperature measurements in a one-dimensional numerical array.
temperatures_c = np.array([15.2, 18.7, 21.4, 24.1])
# NumPy applies this unit conversion to every element of the array at once.
temperatures_k = temperatures_c + 273.15

print("Temperatures in K:", temperatures_k)
print(f"Mean temperature: {temperatures_c.mean():.1f} °C")
print(f"Range: {temperatures_c.min():.1f}–{temperatures_c.max():.1f} °C")

Temperatures in K: [288.35 291.85 294.55 297.25]
Mean temperature: 19.9 °C
Range: 15.2–24.1 °C


The array is useful for a single quantity observed repeatedly. A table with many named variables is better represented by a Pandas DataFrame.
Compared with a native Python list, a NumPy array is designed for numerical work. It supports vectorized calculations—such as adding 273.15 to every temperature—in one clear operation, stores values efficiently, and is much faster for the large arrays used in data analysis and machine learning.

title: Course tools and Python foundations
text:
3. Load the course dataset
The Gas Turbine CO and NOx Emissions dataset records the operation of a gas turbine between 2011 and 2015. It combines ambient conditions, turbine sensor measurements, energy yield, and two emissions outcomes: carbon monoxide (CO) and nitrogen oxides (NOx).
Each row represents one hourly observation of the system: the measured operating and environmental conditions during that hour, together with the emissions observed at that time. This course returns to the same dataset repeatedly so that the modeling choices remain connected to a physical system.
The original data and documentation are available from the UCI Machine Learning Repository.

title: Course tools and Python foundations
text:
5. Make a first plot
A scatter plot helps us inspect whether two variables move together. Each point below is one hourly observation. We draw only a random subset so the plot remains readable.

# Import Matplotlib only when we are ready to make a figure.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Use a readable plotting style for the exploratory figure below.
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")

# Plot a reproducible subset so overlapping points do not hide the overall pattern.
# This is useful for large datasets.
plot_data = data.sample(n=2_000, random_state=4520)

# Each point represents one hourly turbine observation.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.scatter(plot_data["TIT"], plot_data["NOX"], alpha=0.25, s=12)
ax.set(
    xlabel="Turbine inlet temperature, TIT (°C)",
    ylabel="NOx emissions (mg/m³)",
    title="A first view of turbine inlet temperature and NOx emissions",
)
plt.show()

title: Confidence intervals: an interactive coverage simulation
text:
This simulation uses a population we completely know: a normal distribution with population mean \(\mu = 0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\). Each trial draws a new random sample, calculates its sample mean, and creates an approximate 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\).
Throughout this page, \(\mu\) denotes the fixed population mean (the quantity we want to learn), while \(\bar{X}\) denotes the sample mean (our estimate of it).
The dashed vertical line marks the true population mean. Blue intervals contain it; red intervals miss it. A 95% confidence level describes the long-run behavior of this procedure: across many independently constructed intervals, about 95% should contain \(\mu\). It does not guarantee that any particular interval will do so.
For each sample, the simulation constructs the approximate 95% confidence interval
\[
\bar{X} \pm 1.96 \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}},
\]
where \(\bar{X}\) is the sample mean, \(S\) is the sample standard deviation, and \(n\) is the sample size. The sample standard deviation is calculated from the same \(n\) observations:
\[
S = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(X_i - \bar{X}\right)^2}.
\]






TipTry this



Begin with a few intervals, then add more. The occasional red interval makes the meaning of “95% confidence” visible. Reset and repeat: the exact number of misses changes each time, while the long-run pattern remains near 95% coverage.

title: Central Limit Theorem: simulation in Python
text:
The central limit theorem (CLT) explains a surprising pattern: even when individual observations are skewed or discrete, the sample mean often has an approximately normal distribution when the sample size is sufficiently large.
This notebook uses NumPy simulations to make that pattern visible. It is a companion to the browser interactive and is designed to run directly in Google Colab.

title: Central Limit Theorem: simulation in Python
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this notebook, you should be able to:

distinguish one observation, one sample, and a sample mean;
simulate repeated samples from a population;
build the distribution of sample means; and
explain why increasing the sample size changes that distribution, while increasing the number of trials only reveals it more clearly.


import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=4520)

title: Central Limit Theorem: simulation in Python
text:
1. One population, many samples
Suppose a population produces observations denoted by \(X\). A sample contains \(n\) independent observations from that population. Its sample mean is
\[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i.\]
To study how \(\bar{x}\) varies, we repeat the whole sampling process \(B\) times. This gives us \(B\) sample means.

def simulate_sample_means(draw_observations, sample_size, trials, rng):
    """Draw `trials` samples and return the samples and their means."""
    samples = draw_observations(rng, size=(trials, sample_size))
    means = samples.mean(axis=1)
    return samples, means


def show_clt_experiment(draw_observations, sample_size, trials, rng, title):
    """Plot the population, one sample, and all simulated sample means."""
    population_preview = draw_observations(rng, size=10_000)
    samples, means = simulate_sample_means(
        draw_observations, sample_size=sample_size, trials=trials, rng=rng
    )

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.8), constrained_layout=True)
    axes[0].hist(population_preview, bins=35, color="#70a5c8", edgecolor="white")
    axes[0].set(title="Population preview", ylabel="Count")

    axes[1].hist(samples[0], bins=16, color="#d77732", edgecolor="white")
    axes[1].axvline(samples[0].mean(), color="#b65420", linestyle="--", label="sample mean")
    axes[1].set(title=f"One sample (n = {sample_size})")
    axes[1].legend()

    axes[2].hist(means, bins=30, color="#457eaa", edgecolor="white")
    axes[2].axvline(means.mean(), color="#355766", linestyle="--", label="mean of sample means")
    axes[2].set(title=f"Distribution of {trials} sample means")
    axes[2].legend()

    fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=14)
    plt.show()
    return means

title: Central Limit Theorem: simulation in Python
text:
2. A right-skewed population: exponential observations
An exponential distribution can model a waiting time under a simple constant-rate assumption—for example, the time until the next event in a process. It is strongly right-skewed, so it is a useful CLT example.
Start with \(n=1\). In this case, every sample mean is just one observation, so the rightmost plot should look much like the population.

draw_exponential = lambda rng, size: rng.exponential(scale=1, size=size)

means_n1 = show_clt_experiment(
    draw_exponential, sample_size=1, trials=500, rng=rng,
    title="Exponential population with sample size n = 1"
)








Now increase the sample size to \(n=30\). The individual observations are still exponential, but each point in the rightmost plot is now an average of 30 independent observations.

means_n30 = show_clt_experiment(
    draw_exponential, sample_size=30, trials=500, rng=rng,
    title="Exponential population with sample size n = 30"
)

title: Central Limit Theorem: simulation in Python
section: 3. Change the sample size, not the population
text:
3. Change the sample size, not the population
The CLT predicts that the distribution of sample means becomes narrower as \(n\) grows. The standard deviation of the sample mean is called the standard error; under the usual independent-sampling assumption, it decreases in proportion to \(1 / \sqrt{n}\).

sample_sizes = [1, 5, 30, 100]
trials = 1_000

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(sample_sizes), figsize=(15, 3.5), sharey=True, constrained_layout=True)
for ax, sample_size in zip(axes, sample_sizes):
    _, means = simulate_sample_means(draw_exponential, sample_size, trials, rng)
    ax.hist(means, bins=30, color="#457eaa", edgecolor="white")
    ax.axvline(1, color="#355766", linestyle="--")
    ax.set(title=f"n = {sample_size}", xlabel="sample mean")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Count")
fig.suptitle("Exponential population: larger samples give tighter sample means", fontsize=14)
plt.show()

title: Central Limit Theorem: simulation in Python
text:
4. A discrete population: Poisson counts
The CLT does not require continuous observations. A Poisson distribution models a count of events in a fixed interval—for example, the number of detected defects or arrivals during a production interval. Here the population is discrete, but averages of repeated samples can still be approximately normal.

draw_poisson = lambda rng, size: rng.poisson(lam=3, size=size)

poisson_means = show_clt_experiment(
    draw_poisson, sample_size=30, trials=500, rng=rng,
    title="Poisson population (λ = 3) with sample size n = 30"
)

title: Central Limit Theorem: simulation in Python
text:

Replace the Poisson draw function with rng.binomial(n=10, p=0.2, size=size). What does the distribution of sample means look like?

title: Null distributions: an interactive simulation
text:
The null-hypothesis-testing notebook gave us one observed quality-control sample:
\[
n = 25,
\qquad
\bar{X}=20.20\text{ mm},
\qquad
S=0.40\text{ mm}.
\]
We want to know where that one observed sample mean would stand if the null claim (\(H_0: \mu = 20.00\ \text{mm}\)) were true. Choose a null population below, then generate many hypothetical samples of 25 shafts. The resulting distribution of sample means is the null distribution for this test.
The Normal and Uniform models have different shapes for individual shaft diameters, but their displayed parameters give both models the same null mean and population SD. The simulation does not estimate these parameters; it takes them as the specified null model.

title: Data Science for Mechanical Systems
text:
Course focus
Rather than treating machine-learning methods as disconnected algorithms, the course follows a practical engineering progression:

understand engineering data → build predictive models → diagnose systems → learn representations → make decisions and control systems

Students will work repeatedly with a small number of real mechanical-engineering datasets, including gas-turbine emissions and CNC milling tool-wear data. This makes it possible to connect model choices to the systems, sensors, variables, and operating conditions that produced the data.

title: Explore AdaBoost
text:
AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting) builds an ensemble sequentially. It starts with equal weight on every training observation and fits a decision stump: a depth-1 tree with one split. Before fitting the next stump, it gives more weight to the samples the current stump misclassifies. Each later stump therefore pays more attention to earlier mistakes. We use stumps here deliberately to make that mechanism easy to see; AdaBoost can also use deeper trees as its base models.






TipWhat to watch



Add stumps one at a time. Every round uses the same training observations—not a bootstrap sample—but with a new set of observation weights. Compare the weight carried by the samples misclassified by the current stump before and after its update. Then inspect how the stumps cast weighted votes for one new observation and how held-out AUC changes across rounds.



  
    
      Add next stump
      Run all stumps
      Reset
    
    
      Stumps fitted:
      1/12
    
  

  
    
      1
      
        Fit one decision stump using the current weights
        All original training observations remain in the dataset. Their current weights determine how strongly they influence this stump's split.
      
    
    
  

  
    
      2
      
        Give misclassified samples more influence
        The next stump sees the same training samples, but not with equal weight. The samples this stump misclassifies are upweighted.
      
    
    
  

  
    
      3
      
        Pool weighted stump votes for one new observation
A more accurate stump receives a larger vote weight. With each stump prediction \(h_t(\mathbf{x})\) equal to 0 or 1, we compute the normalized positive vote:
\[
s_T(\mathbf{x}) =
\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t h_t(\mathbf{x})}
{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t}.
\]
Because this is a weighted average, \(0 \leq s_T(\mathbf{x}) \leq 1\). It is a ranking score, however—not automatically a calibrated probability.
      
    

    
  

  
    
      4
      
        Evaluate the growing boosted ensemble
        Every intermediate ensemble is evaluated against the same held-out observations. Each point includes all stumps up to that round.
      
    
    
      Held-out AUC as sequential stumps are added
      
    
  


The stump summaries, observation-weight changes, votes, and AUC values are
precomputed from the gas-turbine data. The page reveals real fitted stumps; it
does not train models in the browser.

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
Decision tree is the type of algorithm that generates prediction following a sequence of rules. In this notebook, we will code up a simple decision tree algorithm, to predict whether a gas-turbine operating observation has a high-CO emission.
We will first work through the first two splits using Gini impurity. Then we will turn that logic into a recursive algorithm that can grow a tree to any chosen depth, before comparing it with scikit-learn. The goal is to understand the splitting logic before relying on a library implementation.

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
What is a decision tree?
A decision tree repeatedly divides the observations into smaller regions. Each division asks a yes-or-no question about one feature—for example, whether turbine inlet temperature (TIT) is below a particular value. A new observation follows the applicable branches until it reaches a final region, called a leaf.

The root is the first question, applied to every observation.
An internal node is a later question that applies only to the observations that reached it.
A leaf makes the final prediction. For binary classification, it can report the fraction of positive-label observations in its region, or assign the majority class.

For this notebook, the binary target is represented by the labels 0 and 1.

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
1. Set up the classification task
Each row in the dataset records one gas-turbine operating observation. high_co is our binary target. We offer the tree the measured operating quantities, but exclude CO itself because the target was defined from that measurement.
We reserve 30% of the usable observations as a test set. We will build the tree only with the training observations, then check its simple held-out accuracy at the end.

from pathlib import Path
from urllib.request import urlretrieve

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")

DATA_URL = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/changyaochen/MECE4520/master/"
    "site/data/gas-turbine-course.csv"
)
candidates = [
    Path("../data/gas-turbine-course.csv"),
    Path("site/data/gas-turbine-course.csv"),
    Path("gas-turbine-course.csv"),
]
data_path = next((path for path in candidates if path.exists()), candidates[-1])

# In Google Colab, download the small course dataset if it is not already present.
if not data_path.exists():
    urlretrieve(url=DATA_URL, filename=data_path)

data = pd.read_csv(filepath_or_buffer=data_path)

FEATURES = ["AT", "AP", "AH", "AFDP", "GTEP", "TIT", "TAT", "TEY", "CDP"]
TARGET = "high_co"

# Keep one complete set of measured features for this first implementation.
model_data = data[FEATURES + [TARGET]].dropna().copy()
feature_data = model_data[FEATURES]
target_labels = model_data[TARGET]

# train_test_split accepts its input arrays positionally: features first, labels second.
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    feature_data,
    target_labels,
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=4520,
    stratify=target_labels,

section: 2. Measure class mixing with Gini impurity
text:
2. Measure class mixing with Gini impurity
A tree divides the observations into regions. For a region (R) containing (K) classes, let (p_{R,k}) be the fraction of observations in class (k). The canonical Gini impurity is
\[
G(R) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_{R,k}^{2}.
\]
For our binary target, let (q_R) be the fraction of observations with label 1. The formula becomes
\[
G(R) = 1-q_R^2-(1-q_R)^2 = 2q_R(1-q_R).
\]
It is zero when a region contains only one class, and largest when the two classes are evenly mixed. A classification tree chooses the split that produces the largest reduction in the sample-size-weighted Gini impurity.

def gini_impurity(labels: pd.Series | np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Compute binary Gini impurity for one region.

    Args:
        labels: Binary labels in the region.

    Returns:
        The region's Gini impurity.
    """
    positive_fraction = np.mean(labels)
    return float(2 * positive_fraction * (1 - positive_fraction))


def region_summary(labels: pd.Series | np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float | int | str]:
    """Summarize a region using its observed labels.

    Args:
        labels: Binary labels in the region.

    Returns:
        Sample count, positive-label fraction, Gini impurity, and majority-class label.
    """
    positive_fraction = float(np.mean(labels))
    return {
        "samples": len(labels),
        "positive-label fraction": positive_fraction,
        "Gini impurity": gini_impurity(labels=labels),
        "majority class": 1 if positive_fraction >= 0.5 else 0,
    }

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
3. Score one proposed split
Suppose we propose splitting turbine inlet temperature (TIT) at 1076.95 °C. The observations at or below the cutpoint form the left region; the rest form the right region.
The loss after a split is the weighted average of the two child impurities:
\[
G_{\mathrm{after}} = \frac{n_L}{n}G(R_L) + \frac{n_R}{n}G(R_R).
\]
The resulting Gini decrease is (G(R)-G_{}).

def score_split(
    feature_values: pd.Series, labels: pd.Series, threshold: float
) -> tuple[dict[str, float], pd.Series, pd.Series]:
    """Score one binary cutpoint with weighted Gini impurity.

    Args:
        feature_values: Values of one candidate feature in the parent region.
        labels: Binary labels in the same row order.
        threshold: Values at or below this cutpoint go to the left child.

    Returns:
        Split metrics plus the labels in the left and right child regions.
    """
    left_labels = labels[feature_values <= threshold]
    right_labels = labels[feature_values > threshold]
    n_total = len(labels)

    weighted_child_gini = (
        len(left_labels) / n_total * gini_impurity(labels=left_labels)
        + len(right_labels) / n_total * gini_impurity(labels=right_labels)
    )
    parent_gini = gini_impurity(labels=labels)
    return (
        {
            "parent Gini": parent_gini,
            "weighted child Gini": weighted_child_gini,
            "Gini decrease": parent_gini - weighted_child_gini,
        },
        left_labels,
        right_labels,
    )

proposed_threshold = 1076.95
score, left_labels, right_labels = score_split(
    feature_values=X_train["TIT"],

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
section: 4. Search for the best first split
text:
4. Search for the best first split
Rather than specify one feature and cutpoint ourselves, the tree searches them. For each feature, candidate cutpoints lie halfway between adjacent distinct observed values.
The function below sorts one feature at a time, uses cumulative counts of positive labels, and scores every valid cutpoint. This gives the same greedy search logic as a decision-tree library while keeping the calculation practical for the full training dataset.

def find_best_gini_split(
    features: pd.DataFrame, labels: pd.Series
) -> dict[str, float | int | str]:
    """Find the feature and cutpoint with the smallest weighted Gini impurity.

    Args:
        features: Candidate feature columns for one parent region.
        labels: Binary labels for the same observations.
    Returns:
        Details of the best valid binary split in the region.
    """
    label_values = labels.to_numpy(dtype=int)
    n_samples = len(label_values)
    parent_gini = gini_impurity(labels=label_values)
    best_split: dict[str, float | int | str] | None = None

    for feature_name in features.columns:
        values = features[feature_name].to_numpy()
        order = np.argsort(values, kind="stable")
        sorted_values = values[order]
        sorted_labels = label_values[order]

        # A candidate cutpoint sits between two distinct adjacent values.
        left_sizes = np.arange(1, n_samples)
        right_sizes = n_samples - left_sizes
        left_positive = np.cumsum(sorted_labels)[:-1]
        right_positive = sorted_labels.sum() - left_positive
        valid = sorted_values[:-1] < sorted_values[1:]
        if not valid.any():
            continue

        left_fraction = left_positive / left_sizes
        right_fraction = right_positive / right_sizes
        left_gini = 2 * left_fraction * (1 - left_fraction)
        right_gini = 2 * right_fraction * (1 - right_fraction)
        weighted_gini = (
            left_sizes * left_gini + right_sizes * right_gini
        ) / n_samples

        candidate_index = np.where(valid, weighted_gini, np.inf).argmin()
        candidate_gini = float(weighted_gini[candidate_index])
        if best_split is None or candidate_gini < best_split["weighted child Gini"]:
            best_split = {
                "feature": feature_name,
                "threshold": float(
                    (sorted_values[candidate_index] + sorted_values[candidate_index + 1]) / 2
                ),
                "parent Gini": parent_gini,
                "weighted child Gini": candidate_gini,
                "Gini decrease": parent_gini - candidate_gini,
                "left samples": int(left_sizes[candidate_index]),
                "right samples": int(right_sizes[candidate_index]),
            }

    if best_split is None:
        raise ValueError("No split is available for this region.")
    return best_split

That requires weighting each child region’s local Gini decrease by the fraction of training observations that reach it.
We inspect this second split manually so the selection logic remains easy to follow. The next section generalizes the same search recursively.

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
6. Build a tree recursively
The same split search can be repeated inside every child region. The recursive function below has one hyperparameter: max_depth, the maximum number of decision rules along any path from the root to a leaf. A value of 0 creates one leaf with no rules; a value of 2 permits up to two rules along a path.
The recursion stops when it reaches the requested depth, when all labels in a region agree, when all feature values in a region are identical, or when no split lowers Gini impurity.

def make_leaf(labels: pd.Series) -> dict[str, float | int | bool]:
    """Create a final prediction region.

    Args:
        labels: Binary labels in the final region.

    Returns:
        A dictionary representing one leaf of the tree.
    """
    positive_fraction = float(np.mean(labels))
    return {
        "is_leaf": True,
        "samples": len(labels),
        "positive fraction": positive_fraction,
        "prediction": int(positive_fraction >= 0.5),
    }


def build_tree(
    features: pd.DataFrame,
    labels: pd.Series,
    max_depth: int,
    depth: int = 0,
) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Build a binary classification tree by recursively reducing Gini impurity.

    Args:
        features: Candidate feature columns for the current region.
        labels: Binary labels for the current region.
        max_depth: Maximum number of decision rules from root to leaf.
        depth: Number of rules already used to reach the current region.

    Returns:
        A nested dictionary representing a decision tree.
    """
    no_feature_variation = features.nunique().eq(1).all()
    if (
        depth >= max_depth
        or labels.nunique() == 1
        or no_feature_variation
    ):
        return make_leaf(labels=labels)

    best_split = find_best_gini_split(features=features, labels=labels)
    if best_split["Gini decrease"] <= 0:
        return make_leaf(labels=labels)

    split_feature = str(best_split["feature"])
    split_threshold = float(best_split["threshold"])
    left_mask = features[split_feature] <= split_threshold
    right_mask = ~left_mask

    positive_fraction = float(np.mean(labels))
    return {
        "is_leaf": False,
        "samples": len(labels),
        "positive fraction": positive_fraction,
        "feature": split_feature,
        "threshold": split_threshold,
        "left": build_tree(
            features=features.loc[left_mask],
            labels=labels.loc[left_mask],
            max_depth=max_depth,
            depth=depth + 1,
        ),
        "right": build_tree(
            features=features.loc[right_mask],
            labels=labels.loc[right_mask],
            max_depth=max_depth,
            depth=depth + 1,
        ),
    }


def print_tree(node: dict[str, object], indent: str = "") -> None:
    """Print the decision rules and predictions in a tree.

    Args:
        node: Current node or leaf in the nested tree dictionary.
        indent: Text indentation used to show the tree structure.
    """
    if bool(node["is_leaf"]):
        print(
            f"{indent}Predict {node['prediction']} "
            f"({node['samples']} observations; "
            f"positive fraction = {node['positive fraction']:.3f})"
        )
        return

    feature = str(node["feature"])
    threshold = float(node["threshold"])
    print(f"{indent}If {feature} ≤ {threshold:.3f}:")
    print_tree(node=node["left"], indent=indent + "  ")
    print(f"{indent}Otherwise:")
    print_tree(node=node["right"], indent=indent + "  ")

print_tree(node=scratch_tree)

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
8. Quantify feature importance
The depth-2 tree above is useful for inspecting individual rules, but it contains only a few splits. To make the importance profile richer, we fit a separate tree with max_depth=5. Scikit-learn provides a numerical importance for each feature through the feature_importances_ attribute.

At each split, measure how much the feature makes the child regions less mixed in their labels: the reduction in Gini impurity.
Weight that improvement by the number of observations reaching the split, so a helpful root split matters more than an equally helpful split in a small leaf.
Add these weighted improvements across every split using the same feature, then normalize them so that the importances sum to 1.

A value of 0.70 means that the feature accounts for 70% of this tree’s total weighted Gini reduction. It does not mean that the feature causes 70% of the outcome, or that it accounts for 70% of predictive accuracy. In practice, use held-out performance to choose the tree depth; we use depth 5 here only to make the example more informative.

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
Advanced topics
This shallow tree is deliberately simple so that its rules are easy to inspect. In practice, several extensions matter:

Tree complexity and overfitting. A deep tree can keep adding rules until it memorizes details of the training observations. Parameters such as max_depth, min_samples_split, and min_samples_leaf limit that complexity; choose them by performance on held-out data.
Regression trees. For a continuous target such as NOx, a leaf predicts the average response in its region and splits can be chosen by reduction in mean squared error.
Ensembles. Random forests and gradient-boosted trees combine many trees. They generally predict better than a single tree, at the cost of some interpretability.

title: Decision trees from scratch: classifying gas-turbine operating regions
text:
Takeaways

A classification tree creates regions in feature space and assigns each leaf the majority class. The fraction of positive-label observations in a leaf also provides a simple probability estimate.
Each split greedily reduces weighted Gini impurity. It does not search jointly for every later split.
With max_depth=2, the recursion applies the same greedy split search independently within each child of the root.
Scikit-learn’s feature_importances_ attribute summarizes each feature’s share of the tree’s weighted Gini reduction; it is a predictive description, not a causal measure.
Trees can keep splitting until they memorize training observations, so later we will tune their depth and leaf-size controls using held-out data.

Return to Tree-based

title: How a tree chooses a split
text:
A binary classification tree builds a rule one decision at a time. At each node, it tries candidate cutpoints along every available feature, measures how much each candidate makes the two child regions purer, and selects the largest improvement.






TipFollow the search



This page makes the search explicit. Run the \(x_1\) loop and the \(x_2\) loop for the root node, select the winning split, and then repeat that process for each of its two children. The table records the Gini decrease for every candidate cutpoint that the tree evaluates.


For a region \(R\), the Gini impurity and the decrease from a candidate split are
\[
G(R) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat{p}_{R,k}^{\,2},
\qquad
\Delta G
= G(R) -
\left[
\frac{n_L}{n}G(R_L) + \frac{n_R}{n}G(R_R)
\right].
\]
Here, a larger \(\Delta G\) is better.

title: Random forests: diverse trees, one prediction
text:
A single decision tree can learn useful operating rules, but a small change in its training observations can lead to a different tree. In this notebook, we use many such trees to predict whether a gas-turbine operating observation receives the positive high_co label.
We will first use bagging to average trees fitted to bootstrap samples. A random forest adds another source of diversity: at each split, each tree may consider only a random subset of the available features.

2. Begin with one depth-5 tree
We limit every tree in this notebook to depth 5. An individual depth-5 tree remains flexible, but can still be sensitive to the particular observations it saw. ROC AUC lets us compare the probability rankings on the training and held-out test sets.

def auc_scores(*, model: Any, X_train: pd.DataFrame, y_train: pd.Series, X_test: pd.DataFrame, y_test: pd.Series) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Compute training and held-out ROC AUC for a fitted classifier.

    Args:
        model: A fitted classifier that provides ``predict_proba``.
        X_train: Features used to fit the model.
        y_train: Training labels.
        X_test: Held-out feature values.
        y_test: Held-out labels.

    Returns:
        A dictionary containing training and test ROC AUC values.
    """
    training_probability = model.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]
    test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

    return {
        "training AUC": roc_auc_score(y_train, training_probability),
        "test AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability),
    }

)

section: 3. Bagging: vary the observations, then average
text:
3. Bagging: vary the observations, then average
A bootstrap sample contains the same number of rows as the training set, sampled with replacement. Some observations therefore appear more than once, while others are omitted. Bagging fits one tree to each bootstrap sample.
For a new operating point \(\mathbf{x}\), we average the positive-label probabilities from \(B\) trees:
\[
\hat p_{\mathrm{ensemble}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \hat p_b(\mathbf{x}).
\]

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=RANDOM_STATE)
bootstrap_indices = rng.integers(low=0, high=len(X_train), size=len(X_train))
unique_rows = np.unique(bootstrap_indices).size

print(f"Rows in one bootstrap sample: {len(bootstrap_indices):,}")
print(f"Distinct training rows represented: {unique_rows:,} ({unique_rows / len(X_train):.1%})")

Bagging gives each tree a different bootstrap sample, but every split may still consider all nine features. If one feature is especially attractive, many trees can make very similar early decisions. A random forest breaks that pattern by drawing a fresh subset of feature candidates at every split.

title: Random forests: diverse trees, one prediction
section: 5. Do random feature subsets make trees less alike?
text:
5. Do random feature subsets make trees less alike?
One practical way to compare tree similarity is to correlate their predicted probabilities across the same held-out observations. A high correlation means that two trees tend to assign high and low probabilities to the same observations; a lower correlation means that their predictions differ more.
Each ensemble in this demonstration contains 200 trees. On the 10,620 held-out observations, each tree produces 10,620 predicted probabilities. For every pair of trees, we calculate the Pearson correlation between those two vectors of 10,620 predictions. Collecting every pair gives a \(200 \times 200\) correlation matrix: rows and columns are individual trees, and the diagonal is always 1 because each tree is perfectly correlated with itself. We then remove that diagonal and condense the off-diagonal values into a distribution.
We also inspect the root feature selected by each tree. In bagging, a dominant feature can win at the root of nearly every tree. In a random forest, the feature draw sometimes prevents that feature from competing at all.

def individual_tree_probabilities(*, model: Any, X: pd.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    """Collect positive-label probabilities from every tree in an ensemble.

    Args:
        model: A fitted bagging or random-forest classifier.
        X: Feature values to score.

    Returns:
        An array with one row per observation and one column per tree.
    """
    X_values = X.to_numpy()
    return np.column_stack(
        [tree.predict_proba(X_values)[:, 1] for tree in model.estimators_]
    )


def tree_correlation_matrix(*, probabilities: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Calculate the correlation matrix among ensemble trees.

    Args:
        probabilities: One predicted-probability column per tree.

    Returns:
        A square matrix whose entry (i, j) is the correlation between
        tree i and tree j across the held-out observations.
    """
    return np.corrcoef(probabilities, rowvar=False)


def pairwise_tree_correlations(*, probabilities: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return all unique pairwise correlations among ensemble trees.

    Args:
        probabilities: One predicted-probability column per tree.

    Returns:
        The upper-triangle correlations, excluding the diagonal.
    """
    correlation_matrix = tree_correlation_matrix(probabilities=probabilities)
    upper_triangle = np.triu_indices_from(correlation_matrix, k=1)
    return correlation_matrix[upper_triangle]


def root_feature_names(*, model: Any, feature_names: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Read the feature selected at the root of every fitted tree.

    Args:
        model: A fitted ensemble whose estimators are decision trees.
        feature_names: Feature names in the order supplied to the model.

    Returns:
        The root-split feature from each tree.
    """
    return [feature_names[int(tree.tree_.feature[0])] for tree in model.estimators_]


bagging_tree_probabilities = individual_tree_probabilities(model=bagging, X=X_test)
forest_tree_probabilities = individual_tree_probabilities(model=random_forest, X=X_test)

bagging_correlation_matrix = tree_correlation_matrix(probabilities=bagging_tree_probabilities)
forest_correlation_matrix = tree_correlation_matrix(probabilities=forest_tree_probabilities)
bagging_correlations = pairwise_tree_correlations(probabilities=bagging_tree_probabilities)
forest_correlations = pairwise_tree_correlations(probabilities=forest_tree_probabilities)

bagging_roots = root_feature_names(model=bagging, feature_names=FEATURES)
forest_roots = root_feature_names(model=random_forest, feature_names=FEATURES)

Takeaways

Even a depth-5 tree can be sensitive to its training observations; averaging bootstrap trees makes its predictions much more stable.
Bagging varies the observations available to each tree. A random forest also varies which features compete at each split.
Lower similarity among the trees makes averaging more effective.
A random forest predicts a positive-label probability by averaging the individual tree probabilities.

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
text:
Gradient boosting builds an ensemble sequentially, just as AdaBoost does. But its mechanism is different. To make the idea direct, we use a regression problem: predict continuous NOx concentration from gas-turbine operating measurements.
The model starts with one constant prediction. Each new shallow regression tree then learns a continuous correction to the current prediction.

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
text:
What you will do

Build a high-level mental model of boosting as sequential error correction.
Contrast gradient boosting with bagging and AdaBoost.
Set up one NOx regression task with a fixed train/test split.
Connect residual correction to the word gradient (optional).
Fit small regression trees that supply continuous corrections.
Add the corrections gradually, then evaluate the growing model on the same held-out observations.

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
section: The high-level idea: repair a running forecast
text:
The high-level idea: repair a running forecast
Gradient boosting builds one prediction through a sequence of small revisions. It does not ask every tree to predict NOx from scratch. Instead, each new tree asks: where is the current model still systematically too high or too low?
During training, we repeat this repair loop:

Start from the current prediction for every training observation.
Compare it with the measured NOx and calculate the remaining error.
Fit a small regression tree to recognize operating regions with similar remaining errors.
Add only part of that tree’s correction to the current prediction.
Repeat, so the next tree focuses only on what remains unexplained.

Thus, the final model is an additive model:
\[
\hat{y}^{(T)}(\mathbf{x})
= \overline{y}_{\mathrm{train}}
+ \eta g_1(\mathbf{x})
+ \eta g_2(\mathbf{x})
+ \cdots
+ \eta g_T(\mathbf{x}).
\]
Here, \(\overline{y}_{\mathrm{train}}\) is the initial mean-NOx forecast, each \(g_t(\mathbf{x})\) is the continuous correction supplied by a shallow regression tree, and \(\eta\) retains only a fraction of each correction.

Key idea: a tree in gradient boosting predicts a correction, not a complete NOx value. Many small corrections, added together, form a flexible nonlinear model.

At prediction time, measured NOx is unknown. A new observation simply passes through the already-fitted trees, and the model adds their learned feature-dependent corrections to the baseline.

A tiny staged example
For one training observation, imagine that the current forecast is \(65.0\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}\) while the measured NOx is \(78.0\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}\). The numbers below are illustrative; a real tree learns its correction from many observations with similar operating conditions.

65.9
\(78.0 - 65.9 = +12.1\)

\(78.0 - 66.6 = +11.4\)
\(\cdots\)

The next tree does not redo the entire prediction. It targets the remaining residual after the earlier corrections have already been applied.


How this differs from the earlier ensembles










Method

Main intuition




Bagging / random forest
Independently

Reduce the variance of an unstable tree


AdaBoost

Gradient boosting

So gradient boosting is sequential like AdaBoost, but it is not bootstrap aggregation and it is not sample reweighting. Its next tree is trained on what the current model still gets wrong.

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

1. Set up one regression task
We predict measured NOx concentration using three familiar gas-turbine measurements: ambient temperature (AT), compressor discharge pressure (CDP), and turbine energy yield (TEY). We keep one fixed 70/30 train/test split throughout this notebook. The test observations are never used to fit a correction tree.

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    model_data[FEATURES],
    model_data[TARGET],

    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,

text:
2. Start from one simple forecast
Before fitting any tree, let us predict the same value for every training observation: the average training NOx. It is intentionally crude, but it gives the first correction tree a clear place to start.
For training observation \(i\), the remaining error is its residual:
\[
r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i.
\]
A positive residual means that the current forecast is too low; a negative residual means it is too high. The table below shows two actual training observations. A correction tree will receive every observation’s operating features together with a residual like this one, then look for regions that need similar signed corrections.

def residuals(*, targets: np.ndarray, predictions: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Compute observed-minus-predicted residuals.

    Args:
        targets: Measured target values.
        predictions: Current model predictions.

    Returns:
        One residual per observation.
    """
    return targets - predictions


train_targets = y_train.to_numpy(dtype=float)
test_targets = y_test.to_numpy(dtype=float)
baseline_prediction = float(train_targets.mean())
baseline_train_predictions = np.full(
    shape=len(X_train),
    fill_value=baseline_prediction,
    dtype=float,
)
baseline_test_predictions = np.full(
    shape=len(X_test),
    fill_value=baseline_prediction,
    dtype=float,
)
baseline_residuals = residuals(
    targets=train_targets,
    predictions=baseline_train_predictions,
)

# Select one representative positive and negative residual for display.

    for representative_residual in representative_residuals

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
text:
3. Fit the first correction tree
The first tree is not asked to predict NOx itself. Its training target is the current residual, so its leaf values say how much the baseline prediction should move within each region.
At a boosting stage, the base learner is a regression tree. Its output is a continuous correction, in NOx units, rather than a class label or a probability. Here, the tree is trained to approximate the current residuals.
A depth-1 tree stump would be valid, just as it was for AdaBoost. We use a depth-2 tree here so one correction can distinguish up to four simple operating regions; the depth is a hyperparameter, not a rule. Each terminal-region value shown below is the unshrunk tree output \(g_t(\mathbf{x})\). The learning rate is applied to that output in the next step.
For this first stage, we fit a DecisionTreeRegressor directly. Later, we will use GradientBoostingRegressor to automate the repeated correction process.

LEARNING_RATE = 0.10
MAX_DEPTH = 2
MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF = 50

first_correction_tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(
    max_depth=MAX_DEPTH,
    min_samples_leaf=MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
)
first_correction_tree.fit(X=X_train, y=baseline_residuals)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(15, 6))
plot_tree(
    decision_tree=first_correction_tree,
    feature_names=FEATURES,
    filled=True,
    rounded=True,
    impurity=False,
    precision=2,
    ax=ax,
)
ax.set_title("First depth-2 regression tree: leaf values are NOx corrections (mg/m³)")

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
section: 4. Add the tree’s correction to the current prediction
text:
4. Add the tree’s correction to the current prediction
Let \(g_t(\mathbf{x})\) be the correction supplied by tree \(t\). The update is
\[
\hat{y}_t(\mathbf{x})
= \hat{y}_{t-1}(\mathbf{x})
+ \eta g_t(\mathbf{x}),
\]
where \(\eta\) is the learning rate. It shrinks each correction so one tree does not change the model too aggressively. Here, \(\eta = 0.10\).
For a genuinely new observation, its measured NOx value is unknown. The tree selects \(g_t(\mathbf{x})\) using only its features. In the worked held-out example below, we reveal the measured NOx afterward so that we can compare the evolving prediction with the ground truth.

first_tree_correction = first_correction_tree.predict(X=X_train)

    baseline_train_predictions + LEARNING_RATE * first_tree_correction
)

    "Training MSE before / after the first correction: "
    f"{mean_squared_error(y_true=train_targets, y_pred=baseline_train_predictions):.2f}"
    " / "
    f"{mean_squared_error(y_true=train_targets, y_pred=manual_first_predictions):.2f}"
)

    first_correction_tree.predict(X=example_features)[0]
)

    example_prediction_before + LEARNING_RATE * example_tree_correction

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
text:
5. Repeat the correction process
We have now carried out one boosting step by hand: fit a tree to the current residuals, shrink its correction, and add it to the forecast. Next, GradientBoostingRegressor automates 60 repetitions of that same loop. At every stage, the next tree sees the residuals left by all earlier trees and adds another shrunk correction. We evaluate every intermediate model on the same test data.

def staged_metrics(
    *,
    model: GradientBoostingRegressor,
    training_features: pd.DataFrame,
    training_targets: pd.Series,
    test_features: pd.DataFrame,
    test_targets: pd.Series,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Measure regression performance after each boosting stage.

    Args:
        model: A fitted gradient-boosting regressor.
        training_features: Feature table used to fit the model.
        training_targets: Continuous training targets.
        test_features: Held-out feature table.
        test_targets: Continuous held-out targets.

    Returns:
        One row per boosting stage with training/test MSE and test R-squared.
    """
    rows = []
    staged_training_predictions = model.staged_predict(X=training_features)
    staged_test_predictions = model.staged_predict(X=test_features)
    for stage, (training_prediction, test_prediction) in enumerate(
        zip(
            staged_training_predictions,
            staged_test_predictions,
            strict=True,
        ),
        start=1,
    ):
        rows.append(
            {
                "Stage": stage,
                "Training MSE": mean_squared_error(
                    y_true=training_targets,
                    y_pred=training_prediction,
                ),
                "Test MSE": mean_squared_error(
                    y_true=test_targets,
                    y_pred=test_prediction,
                ),
                "Test R²": r2_score(
                    y_true=test_targets,
                    y_pred=test_prediction,
                ),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


boosted_model = GradientBoostingRegressor(
    loss="squared_error",
    n_estimators=60,
    learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,
    max_depth=MAX_DEPTH,

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
text:
6. The main knobs and takeaways

Learning rate \(\eta\) controls the size of each correction. A smaller value usually requires more trees.
Number of trees controls how long the sequential process runs. We use held-out performance to decide when additional corrections stop helping.
Tree depth and minimum leaf size control the flexibility of each correction tree. Deeper trees can learn more complex corrections, but they also make overfitting easier.

A shallow tree can identify one broad, simple error pattern. The next tree is then free to explain a different pattern left behind. Many small, learning-rate-shrunk corrections can represent a complex response while we monitor held-out performance and stop before overfitting.
AdaBoost and gradient boosting are both sequential ensembles, but their training mechanisms differ:

AdaBoost: reweights samples that earlier classifier stumps misclassify, then takes a weighted vote.
Gradient boosting: fits regression trees to current residuals (more generally, negative loss gradients) and adds their continuous corrections.

title: Gradient boosting: correct the current model
text:
7. (Optional) Why gradient boosting?
We have built a model by adding small corrections to its predictions. Let’s connect that process to the gradient descent we already know: both methods start with an initial guess and accumulate steps that aim to reduce a loss.

1. Ordinary gradient descent: accumulate parameter updates
In ordinary gradient descent, we search for parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) that minimize \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\). Starting from an initial guess \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\), we repeatedly use the familiar update:
\[
\boldsymbol{\theta}_t
= \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}
- \eta\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}).
\]
Let’s name the change made at iteration \(t\):
\[
\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_t
= -\eta\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\theta}_t
= \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1} + \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_t.
\]
After \(T\) iterations, the final parameter vector is the initial guess plus all the changes we have accumulated:
\[
\boldsymbol{\theta}_T
= \boldsymbol{\theta}_0
+ \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_1
+ \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_2
+ \cdots
+ \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_T
= \boldsymbol{\theta}_0
+ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_t.
\]
Each step changes the parameters of the same model. The gradient is recomputed at the current parameters, so the direction can change from one iteration to the next.


2. Gradient boosting: accumulate prediction-function updates
Now let’s search for a prediction function \(F\) that minimizes \(\mathcal{L}(F)\). In our regression example, \(F(\mathbf{x})\) predicts NOx. We start with the constant function \(F_0(\mathbf{x})=\bar{y}_{\mathrm{train}}\). At each stage, we ask: how should the current predictions change to reduce the loss? This is the function-space version of asking how the parameters should change.
The negative gradient gives a desired correction at each training input. Those corrections can have a closed-form expression—we will derive them below. But a list of corrections for the training observations does not yet tell us how to correct a prediction for a new input. We fit a regression tree \(g_t(\mathbf{x})\) to these targets so it learns a correction as a function of the features.
With learning rate \(\eta\), our function update is
\[
\Delta F_t(\mathbf{x}) = \eta g_t(\mathbf{x}),
\qquad
F_t(\mathbf{x})
= F_{t-1}(\mathbf{x}) + \eta g_t(\mathbf{x}).
\]
Here, \(F_t\) is the entire ensemble prediction function after \(t\) trees; \(g_t\) is the new tree added at that stage. Expanding the updates gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_1(\mathbf{x}) &= F_0(\mathbf{x}) + \eta g_1(\mathbf{x}), \\
F_2(\mathbf{x}) &= F_0(\mathbf{x}) + \eta g_1(\mathbf{x})
+ \eta g_2(\mathbf{x}), \\
F_T(\mathbf{x}) &= F_0(\mathbf{x})
+ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta F_t(\mathbf{x})
= F_0(\mathbf{x}) + \eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}g_t(\mathbf{x}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Just as \(\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_t\) is a step in parameter space, \(\eta g_t\) is a step in prediction-function space. A shallow tree can only represent certain patterns of corrections, so it approximates the negative-gradient direction. After adding it, we recompute the correction targets using the updated ensemble before fitting the next tree.







Ordinary gradient descent
Gradient boosting

Start from \(F_0\)


Compute a parameter update \(\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_t\) from the gradient
Learn a function update \(\Delta F_t=\eta g_t\) from negative-gradient targets

Add the correction tree to the current function


Accumulate parameter updates
Accumulate learned correction functions





3. Squared-error regression: where do the correction targets come from?
For the mean squared-error objective, written in terms of the prediction function,
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}(F)
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i - F(\mathbf{x}_i)\right]^2.
\]
The derivative is taken with respect to the function’s value at a particular training input, \(F(\mathbf{x}_i)\):
\[
-\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}(F)}
{\partial F(\mathbf{x}_i)}
= \frac{2}{n}\left[y_i - F(\mathbf{x}_i)\right].
\]
At stage \(t\), define the current residual as
\[
r_i^{(t)}
= y_i - F_{t-1}(\mathbf{x}_i).
\]
If we collect the current predictions into \(\mathbf{f}=[F(\mathbf{x}_1),\ldots,F(\mathbf{x}_n)]^T\), the negative gradient over these \(n\) predictions is
\[
-\nabla_{\mathbf{f}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}(F)
= \frac{2}{n}
\begin{bmatrix}
r_1^{(t)} \\
r_2^{(t)} \\
\vdots \\
r_n^{(t)}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Therefore, the residual vector points in exactly the same direction as the negative gradient; the positive constant \(2/n\) only changes its scale and can be absorbed into the learning rate. The next tree is fitted to these residuals:
\[
g_t
= \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{g\in\mathcal{G}}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[r_i^{(t)} - g(\mathbf{x}_i)\right]^2,
\]
where \(\mathcal{G}\) is the family of allowed regression trees. The tree is an approximation to the unrestricted, observation-by-observation negative gradient because it cannot prescribe an independent change for every training observation. Instead, it identifies feature regions that need similar corrections. This is why the residual-fitting loop we implemented earlier is a form of gradient descent: each fitted tree supplies the next function update, using the residuals as its negative-gradient targets.


4. Binary classification: the same process with a different loss
For binary classification, gradient boosting still adds regression-tree corrections. We maintain an unbounded score \(F(\mathbf{x})\), then convert it to a probability with the sigmoid function:
\[
p_i = \sigma\!\left(F(\mathbf{x}_i)\right)
= \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left[-F(\mathbf{x}_i)\right]}.
\]
Using binary cross-entropy,
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}(F)
= -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right],
\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\},
\]
the negative gradient with respect to the score is
\[
-\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}(F)}
{\partial F(\mathbf{x}_i)}
= \frac{1}{n}\left(y_i-p_i\right).
\]
Thus the next regression tree is fitted to the continuous pseudo-residual
\[
q_i^{(t)}
= y_i - p_i^{(t-1)},
\qquad
p_i^{(t-1)}
= \sigma\!\left(F_{t-1}(\mathbf{x}_i)\right).
\]
The sign of \(q_i^{(t)}\) is fixed by the label: it is positive when \(y_i=1\) and negative when \(y_i=0\). Its magnitude is the useful information. For a positive-label sample, \(p_i^{(t-1)}\approx 0\) gives \(q_i^{(t)}\approx 1\) and calls for a large upward correction, whereas \(p_i^{(t-1)}\approx 1\) gives \(q_i^{(t)}\approx 0\). Likewise, a negative-label sample with \(p_i^{(t-1)}\approx 1\) has \(q_i^{(t)}\approx -1\) and calls for a large downward correction; when \(p_i^{(t-1)}\approx 0\), its correction is near zero. The update remains
\[
F_t(\mathbf{x})
= F_{t-1}(\mathbf{x}) + \eta g_t(\mathbf{x}),
\qquad
p_t(\mathbf{x})
= \sigma\!\left(F_t(\mathbf{x})\right).
\]
The tree changes the raw score, not the probability directly. In practical implementations, the tree’s terminal values may receive an additional loss-based optimization; the central first-order idea remains the same: each new tree approximates the negative gradient of the current loss.

The connection: ordinary gradient descent accumulates changes to the parameters. Gradient boosting accumulates learned changes to the prediction function. The loss determines the correction targets at each stage.

title: Ranking and probability quality
text: The previous notebook evaluated an alert decision after choosing a probability threshold. A classifier also produces probability scores that we can evaluate without fixing one threshold. Here, we separate three questions:

title: Ranking and probability quality
text:
1. Fit the TIT-based probability model
As before, each row is one gas-turbine operating observation. The target high_co equals 1 when measured CO is at least 2 mg/m³. We train logistic regression with turbine inlet temperature (TIT) as its one feature, then keep a test set for comparison.

from pathlib import Path
from urllib.request import urlretrieve

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (
    log_loss,
    precision_recall_curve,
    roc_auc_score,
    roc_curve,
)
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")

DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/changyaochen/MECE4520/master/site/data/gas-turbine-course.csv"
candidates = [
    Path("../data/gas-turbine-course.csv"),
    Path("site/data/gas-turbine-course.csv"),
    Path("gas-turbine-course.csv"),
]
data_path = next((path for path in candidates if path.exists()), candidates[-1])

# In Google Colab, download the small course dataset if it is not already present.
if not data_path.exists():
    urlretrieve(DATA_URL, data_path)

data = pd.read_csv(data_path)
model_data = data[["TIT", "high_co"]].dropna().copy()
X = model_data[["TIT"]]
y = model_data["high_co"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.30, random_state=4520, stratify=y
)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1_000).fit(X_train, y_train)
train_probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]
test_probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

title: Ranking and probability quality
section: 2. Trace precision, recall, and F1 across thresholds
text:
2. Trace precision, recall, and F1 across thresholds
The previous notebook calculated precision, recall, and F1 after choosing one alert threshold. Here, we sweep the same threshold \(\tau\) from strict to permissive and watch those quantities change.
\[
\operatorname{Precision}(\tau) =
\frac{TP(\tau)}{TP(\tau)+FP(\tau)},
\qquad
\operatorname{Recall}(\tau) =
\frac{TP(\tau)}{TP(\tau)+FN(\tau)}.
\]
Precision asks: among the observations labeled high CO, how many actually have high CO? Recall asks: among all actual high-CO observations, how many did we find? Lowering \(\tau\) usually increases recall, but it can decrease precision as more false alerts are included.
The F1 score summarizes their balance:
\[
F_1(\tau) =
\frac{2\,\operatorname{Precision}(\tau)\,
\operatorname{Recall}(\tau)}
{\operatorname{Precision}(\tau)+\operatorname{Recall}(\tau)}.
\]
The two plots below use the training predictions so they match the interactive explorer. The horizontal reference line is the fraction of high-CO observations in the training data; it is the precision from labeling every observation positive.

train_precision, train_recall, train_thresholds = precision_recall_curve(
    y_train, train_probabilities
)

# Precision and recall include one endpoint with no matching threshold.
train_f1 = np.divide(
    2 * train_precision[:-1] * train_recall[:-1],
    train_precision[:-1] + train_recall[:-1],
    out=np.zeros_like(train_thresholds),
    where=(train_precision[:-1] + train_recall[:-1]) != 0,
)

fig, (ax_pr, ax_f1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5))

ax_pr.plot(
    train_recall,
    train_precision,
    color="#3F78A8",
    linewidth=2.5,
    label="Training precision–recall curve",
)
ax_pr.axhline(
    y_train.mean(),
    color="#5F6368",
    linestyle="--",
    label=f"High-CO fraction = {y_train.mean():.3f}",
)

for threshold, color in [(0.20, "#E1812C"), (0.50, "#1B4F72")]:
    predicted_labels = (train_probabilities >= threshold).astype(int)
    precision_value = (predicted_labels[y_train.to_numpy() == 1].sum()
                       / predicted_labels.sum())
    recall_value = predicted_labels[y_train.to_numpy() == 1].mean()
    f1_value = 2 * precision_value * recall_value / (precision_value + recall_value)

    ax_pr.scatter(
        recall_value,
        precision_value,
        color=color,
        edgecolor="white",
        linewidth=1.3,
        s=90,
        zorder=3,
    )
    ax_f1.scatter(
        threshold,
        f1_value,
        color=color,
        edgecolor="white",
        linewidth=1.3,
        s=90,
        zorder=3,
        label=rf"$\tau={threshold:.1f}$: F1 = {f1_value:.3f}",
    )

ax_pr.set(
    xlabel="Recall",
    ylabel="Precision",
    title="Precision–recall trade-off",
    xlim=(0, 1),
    ylim=(0, 1.03),
)
ax_pr.legend(loc="lower left", frameon=True)

ax_f1.plot(
    train_thresholds,
    train_f1,
    color="#3F78A8",
    linewidth=2.5,
)
ax_f1.set(
    xlabel=r"Decision threshold $\tau$",
    ylabel="F1 score",
    title="F1 depends on the threshold",
    xlim=(0, 1),
    ylim=(0, 1.03),
)
ax_f1.legend(loc="lower center", frameon=True)
plt.show()

title: Ranking and probability quality
section: 3. Measure ranking with ROC and area under the curve (AUC)
text:
3. Measure ranking with ROC and area under the curve (AUC)
At a threshold \(\tau\), the true-positive rate and false-positive rate are
\[
\operatorname{TPR}(\tau) = \frac{TP(\tau)}{TP(\tau)+FN(\tau)},
\qquad
\operatorname{FPR}(\tau) = \frac{FP(\tau)}{FP(\tau)+TN(\tau)}.
\]
An ROC curve traces TPR against FPR as \(\tau\) moves from a strict threshold to a permissive one. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarizes ranking quality: it is the chance that the model assigns a randomly chosen high-CO observation a higher score than a randomly chosen not-high-CO observation. An AUC of 0.5 corresponds to random ranking.

train_fpr, train_tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_train, train_probabilities)
test_fpr, test_tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, test_probabilities)
train_auc = roc_auc_score(y_train, train_probabilities)
test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probabilities)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 7.2))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="#5F6368",
        label="Random ranking (AUC = 0.500)")
ax.plot(train_fpr, train_tpr, color="#3F78A8", linewidth=2.5,
        label=f"Training ROC (AUC = {train_auc:.3f})")
ax.plot(test_fpr, test_tpr, color="#E1812C", linewidth=2.5,
        label=f"Test ROC (AUC = {test_auc:.3f})")
ax.set(
    xlabel="False-positive rate (FPR)",
    ylabel="True-positive rate (TPR)",
    title="TIT provides useful ranking of high-CO observations",
    xlim=(0, 1),
    ylim=(0, 1),
    aspect="equal",
)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=True)
plt.show()








Explore how the ROC curve, precision–recall curve, and F1 score change together as the threshold moves.

title: Ranking and probability quality
section: 4. Measure probability quality with log loss
text:
4. Measure probability quality with log loss
AUC only cares about the ordering of scores. It does not check whether a predicted probability such as 0.90 is numerically credible. For that, we use the binary cross-entropy introduced with logistic regression, often called log loss:
\[
\operatorname{LogLoss} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(\hat p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat p_i)\right].
\]
To make this scale interpretable, compare it with the loss from predicting the test-set high-CO fraction \(\bar y\) for every observation:
\[
H(\bar y) = -\bar y\log(\bar y) - (1-\bar y)\log(1-\bar y),
\qquad
\text{normalized log loss} = \frac{\operatorname{LogLoss}}{H(\bar y)}.
\]
A normalized log loss of 1 means the model is no better than this constant-probability baseline; lower values are better.

# Make deliberately overconfident predictions without changing their rank.
test_scores = model.decision_function(X_test)
sharpened_probabilities = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-5 * test_scores))

test_prevalence = y_test.mean()
baseline_log_loss = -(
    test_prevalence * np.log(test_prevalence)
    + (1 - test_prevalence) * np.log(1 - test_prevalence)
)

probability_quality = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "AUC": [
            roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probabilities),
            roc_auc_score(y_test, sharpened_probabilities),
        ],
        "log loss": [
            log_loss(y_test, test_probabilities),
            log_loss(y_test, sharpened_probabilities),
        ],
    },
    index=["Original TIT model", "Overconfident $5z$ scores"],
)
probability_quality["normalized log loss"] = (
    probability_quality["log loss"] / baseline_log_loss
)
probability_quality.style.format(
    {"AUC": "{:.3f}", "log loss": "{:.3f}",
     "normalized log loss": "{:.3f}"}
)






 
AUC
log loss
normalized log loss




Original TIT model
0.871
0.412
0.617


Overconfident $5z$ scores
0.871
1.011
1.514





Multiplying every log-odds score \(z_i\) by 5 is strictly increasing, so it preserves the ranking and therefore AUC. But it moves probabilities closer to 0 and 1. When the model is wrong, it is now much more confidently wrong, which log loss penalizes heavily.

title: Ranking and probability quality
section: 5. Check calibration with a reliability diagram
text:
5. Check calibration with a reliability diagram
Calibration asks whether the probability values mean what they say. For example, among test observations assigned probabilities near 0.70, we would hope that approximately 70% actually have high CO. A reliability diagram bins the predicted probabilities and compares their mean with the observed high-CO fraction in each bin.

def reliability_points(labels, probabilities, n_bins=10):
    """Return observed fractions and mean predictions in probability bins."""
    observed_fraction, mean_prediction = calibration_curve(
        labels, probabilities, n_bins=n_bins, strategy="uniform"
    )
    return observed_fraction, mean_prediction


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 7.2))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="#5F6368",
        label="Perfect calibration")
for labels, probabilities, label, color, marker in [
    (y_train, train_probabilities, "Training set", "#3F78A8", "o"),
    (y_test, test_probabilities, "Test set", "#E1812C", "s"),
]:
    observed_fraction, mean_prediction = reliability_points(labels, probabilities)
    ax.plot(mean_prediction, observed_fraction, color=color, marker=marker,
            markersize=7, linewidth=2.5, label=label)

ax.set(
    xlabel="Mean predicted probability",
    ylabel="Observed high-CO fraction",
    title="Reliability of TIT-based high-CO probabilities",
    xlim=(0, 1),
    ylim=(0, 1),
    aspect="equal",
)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=True)
plt.show()

title: Ranking and probability quality
section: 6. Choose the metric that answers the question
text:
6. Choose the metric that answers the question







Question
Useful evaluation

ROC and AUC: ranking quality

title: Logistic regression and gradient descent
text:
In the likelihood notebook, we selected the probability that best explained a set of red/blue ticket draws. Here, we use the same maximum-likelihood idea to fit a logistic-regression model for gas-turbine operating observations.
In the data, each row records one operating observation. Our target is the course-defined high-CO label: it is 1 when CO is at least 2 mg/m³ and 0 otherwise. We will use turbine inlet temperature (TIT) as one feature and implement gradient descent ourselves.
from pathlib import Path

title: Logistic regression and gradient descent
text:
2. A logistic probability model
Let \(y_i\) be the high-CO label for observation \(i\). We first standardize TIT, then map a linear score to a probability with the sigmoid function:
\[
\tilde{x}_i = \frac{\mathrm{TIT}_i-\overline{\mathrm{TIT}}}{s_{\mathrm{TIT}}},
\qquad
z_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\tilde{x}_i,
\qquad
p_i=P(y_i=1\mid \tilde{x}_i)=\sigma(z_i)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z_i}}.
\]
Standardizing TIT is not a different model. It is a convenient re-expression of the same feature: \(\beta_1\) now describes a one-standard-deviation change in TIT, and a single learning rate can update both coefficients sensibly.

tit_mean = model_data["TIT"].mean()
tit_std = model_data["TIT"].std(ddof=0)
model_data["tit_standardized"] = (model_data["TIT"] - tit_mean) / tit_std

# The first column of X supplies the intercept; the second is standardized TIT.
X = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(model_data)),
    model_data["tit_standardized"].to_numpy(),
])
y = model_data["high_co"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

def sigmoid(z: float | np.ndarray) -> float | np.ndarray:
    """Map linear score(s) to probability values.

    Args:
        z: A scalar or NumPy array of linear scores.

    Returns:
        The corresponding probability or array of probabilities in [0, 1].
    """
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

print(f"Mean TIT: {tit_mean:.2f} °C")
print(f"Standard deviation of TIT: {tit_std:.2f} °C")
print(f"Design-matrix shape: {X.shape}")

title: Logistic regression and gradient descent
section: 3. Turn likelihood into a loss function
text:
3. Turn likelihood into a loss function
For independent binary observations, maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the average negative log-likelihood, also called binary cross-entropy:
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
\]
Smaller values mean that the model assigns higher probability to the labels we actually observed. To minimize this loss, we also need its gradient with respect to the coefficient vector:
\[
\mathbf{p}=\sigma(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}),
\qquad
\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y}).
\]
Here, \(\mathbf{X}\) is the design matrix, \(\mathbf{p}\) contains the predicted probabilities, and \(\mathbf{y}\) contains the observed 0/1 labels. The vector \(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y}\) measures each prediction’s error; multiplying by \(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\) combines those errors into one update direction for the two coefficients.
The loss_and_gradient function below follows that sequence:

Compute one linear score for each observation.
Transform the scores into predicted probabilities with the sigmoid.
Compute and average the per-observation binary cross-entropy losses.
Combine the probability errors into the gradient above.

The code below follows the displayed expression directly. It clips probabilities only to prevent taking the logarithm of 0 if floating-point roundoff produces an extreme value of exactly 0 or 1.

def loss_and_gradient(
    beta: np.ndarray, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray
) -> tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
    """Compute binary cross-entropy and its gradient.

    Args:
        beta: Current intercept and standardized-TIT slope, shape (2,).
        X: Design matrix with intercept and standardized-TIT columns.
        y: Observed high-CO labels, encoded as zeros and ones.

    Returns:
        A pair containing the average binary cross-entropy and its
        gradient with respect to `beta`.
    """
    # One linear score and one predicted probability per observation.
    scores = X @ beta
    probabilities = sigmoid(scores)

    # Keep logarithms defined if floating-point roundoff produces 0 or 1.
    safe_probabilities = np.clip(probabilities, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    per_observation_loss = -(
        y * np.log(safe_probabilities)
        + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - safe_probabilities)
    )
    loss = np.mean(per_observation_loss)

    # Weight probability errors by the feature values, then average them.
    probability_errors = probabilities - y
    gradient = X.T @ probability_errors / len(y)
    return float(loss), gradient

initial_beta = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
initial_loss, initial_gradient = loss_and_gradient(initial_beta, X, y)

print("At β₀ = β₁ = 0, every predicted probability is 0.5.")
print(f"Initial BCE: {initial_loss:.4f}")
print(f"Gradient: {initial_gradient}")

title: Logistic regression and gradient descent
text:
4. One gradient-descent update
The gradient introduced above points in the direction of greatest local increase in the loss. To decrease the loss, we step in the opposite direction:
\[
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}
=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}-\eta\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}
\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}\right).
\]
Here, \(\eta\) is the learning rate. It controls how far one update travels. We begin at \((0,0)\) and use \(\eta=0.75\).

learning_rate = 0.75
one_step_beta = initial_beta - learning_rate * initial_gradient
one_step_loss, _ = loss_and_gradient(one_step_beta, X, y)

print(f"Start: β = {initial_beta}, BCE = {initial_loss:.4f}")
print(f"After one step: β = {one_step_beta.round(3)}, BCE = {one_step_loss:.4f}")

Start: β = [0. 0.], BCE = 0.6931
After one step: β = [-0.084 -0.24 ], BCE = 0.6151

title: Logistic regression and gradient descent
text:
5. Repeat the updates
A complete gradient-descent fit repeats the same calculation many times. The history records the coefficient values and loss after every iteration, including the starting point.
For a fixed learning rate, the algorithm is:

Start with an initial coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(0)}\).
Compute the predicted probabilities and the loss gradient.
Move one step opposite the gradient.
Repeat until the loss and coefficients no longer change much.


def gradient_descent(
    X: np.ndarray,
    y: np.ndarray,
    learning_rate: float = 0.75,
    n_steps: int = 100,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Fit logistic-regression coefficients with gradient descent.

    Args:
        X: Design matrix with intercept and standardized-TIT columns.
        y: Observed high-CO labels, encoded as zeros and ones.
        learning_rate: Size of each update opposite the gradient.
        n_steps: Number of coefficient updates to perform.

    Returns:
        A pair containing the final coefficient vector and a table with
        the coefficient values and BCE at every iteration.
    """
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    history = []

    for iteration in range(n_steps + 1):
        loss, gradient = loss_and_gradient(beta, X, y)
        history.append({
            "iteration": iteration,
            "beta_0": beta[0],
            "beta_1": beta[1],
            "bce": loss,
        })

        if iteration < n_steps:
            beta = beta - learning_rate * gradient

    return beta, pd.DataFrame(history)

beta_hat, history = gradient_descent(X, y, learning_rate=learning_rate, n_steps=100)

section: 6. Return to the raw TIT scale
text:
6. Return to the raw TIT scale
The optimization used standardized TIT, but we can draw the fitted probability curve against the original TIT values. If
\[
p_i=\sigma(\beta_0+\beta_1\tilde{x}_i),
\]
then the equivalent raw-TIT coefficients are
\[
b_1=\frac{\beta_1}{s_{\mathrm{TIT}}},
\qquad
b_0=\beta_0-\frac{\beta_1\overline{\mathrm{TIT}}}{s_{\mathrm{TIT}}}.
\]
The fitted curve gives a probability, not a promise that each individual 0/1 observation will match the curve.

raw_slope = beta_hat[1] / tit_std
raw_intercept = beta_hat[0] - beta_hat[1] * tit_mean / tit_std

print(f"Standardized-scale fit: β₀ = {beta_hat[0]:.3f}, β₁ = {beta_hat[1]:.3f}")
print(f"Raw-TIT fit: log-odds = {raw_intercept:.3f} + ({raw_slope:.5f}) × TIT")

tit_grid = np.linspace(model_data["TIT"].min(), model_data["TIT"].max(), 400)
standardized_grid = (tit_grid - tit_mean) / tit_std
probability_grid = sigmoid(beta_hat[0] + beta_hat[1] * standardized_grid)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
ax.scatter(
    plot_data["TIT"],
    label_jitter,
    s=14,
    alpha=0.12,
    color="#457eaa",
    edgecolor="none",
    label="Operating observations",
)
ax.plot(tit_grid, probability_grid, color="#c43c35", linewidth=3, label="Fitted high-CO probability")
ax.set(
    xlabel="Turbine inlet temperature, TIT (°C)",
    ylabel="High-CO label or predicted probability",
    yticks=[0, 1],
    ylim=(-0.12, 1.12),
    title="The fitted probability declines as TIT increases",
