title: Neural networks: forward propagation
section: 2. Define a network with one hidden layer
text:
2. Define a network with one hidden layer
Our network has three hidden units and one output unit. For a batch of inputs, the forward pass is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Z}^{[1]} &= \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{W}^{[1]})^T+\mathbf{B}^{[1]},\\
\mathbf{A}^{[1]} &= \operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{Z}^{[1]}),\\
\mathbf{Z}^{[2]} &= \mathbf{A}^{[1]}(\mathbf{W}^{[2]})^T+\mathbf{B}^{[2]},\\
\hat{\mathbf{p}} &= \sigma(\mathbf{Z}^{[2]}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here, each row of \(\mathbf{W}^{[1]}\) holds the nine weights for one hidden unit, so \(\mathbf{W}^{[1]}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times9}\). Similarly, \(\mathbf{W}^{[2]}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times3}\) maps the three hidden activations to one output score. For this batch, \(\mathbf{B}^{[1]}\in
\mathbb{R}^{4\times3}\) and \(\mathbf{B}^{[2]}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times1}\) repeat the learned biases for each observation. The sigmoid converts each final score to a number between 0 and 1.

def sigmoid(values: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Map output scores to values between zero and one.

    Args:
        values: Array of real-valued output scores.

    Returns:
        Array with the same shape as `values`, with entries in [0, 1].
    """
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-values))


def relu(values: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Apply the rectified linear-unit activation elementwise.

    Args:
        values: Array of hidden-layer scores.

    Returns:
        Array with negative entries replaced by zero.
    """
    return np.maximum(values, 0)


def identity(values: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return hidden-layer scores unchanged.

    Args:
        values: Array of hidden-layer scores.

    Returns:
        The input array, unchanged.
    """
    return values


# A fixed seed makes this random example reproducible. These parameters have
# not been fitted to the gas-turbine labels.
N_HIDDEN_UNITS = 3
rng = np.random.default_rng(4520)

# This follows the slide convention: each row gives one unit's weights.
weights_hidden = rng.normal(
    loc=0.0, scale=0.6, size=(N_HIDDEN_UNITS, len(FEATURES))
)
hidden_bias_per_unit = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=0.15, size=N_HIDDEN_UNITS)
weights_output = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=0.6, size=(1, N_HIDDEN_UNITS))
output_bias = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=0.15, size=1)

# The slide writes B[1] and B[2] with one row for every observation.
bias_hidden = np.broadcast_to(
    hidden_bias_per_unit, (X_batch.shape[0], N_HIDDEN_UNITS)
)
bias_output = np.broadcast_to(output_bias, (X_batch.shape[0], 1))

The hidden activations now have three columns, one for each hidden unit. Multiply them by the transposed output weights, add \(\mathbf{B}^{[2]}\), and apply the sigmoid to obtain a probability for each observation.

Package the calculation in a function
The two cells above are the complete forward pass. Now that each operation is visible, we can wrap the same sequence in a reusable function. The function should give exactly the same arrays as the explicit calculation.

def forward_pass(
    *,
    X: np.ndarray,
    weights_hidden: np.ndarray,
    bias_hidden: np.ndarray,
    weights_output: np.ndarray,
    bias_output: np.ndarray,
    activation: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray],
) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Compute one forward pass through a one-hidden-layer network.

    Args:
        X: Input feature matrix with shape (n_observations, n_features).
        weights_hidden: Hidden-layer weights with shape
            (n_hidden_units, n_features).
        bias_hidden: Broadcast hidden biases, with shape
            (n_observations, n_hidden_units).
        weights_output: Output-layer weights with shape
            (1, n_hidden_units).
        bias_output: Broadcast output bias with shape
            (n_observations, 1).
        activation: Elementwise hidden-layer activation function.

    Returns:
        Dictionary containing the hidden scores, hidden activations, output
        scores, and positive-label probabilities.
    """
    hidden_scores = X @ weights_hidden.T + bias_hidden
    hidden_activations = activation(hidden_scores)
    output_scores = hidden_activations @ weights_output.T + bias_output
    probabilities = sigmoid(output_scores)

    return {
        "hidden_scores": hidden_scores,
        "hidden_activations": hidden_activations,
        "output_scores": output_scores,
        "probabilities": probabilities,
    }


relu_outputs = forward_pass(
    X=X_batch,
    weights_hidden=weights_hidden,
    bias_hidden=bias_hidden,
    weights_output=weights_output,
    bias_output=bias_output,
    activation=relu,
)

)

title: Neural networks: forward propagation
section: 3. Trace one observation through the network
text:
3. Trace one observation through the network
For one observation, each hidden unit first forms a weighted sum of the nine standardized inputs. ReLU keeps a positive score and replaces a negative score with zero. The output unit then combines the three hidden activations into one score and one probability.

OBSERVATION_POSITION = 2
source_row = BATCH_ROWS[OBSERVATION_POSITION]

observation_inputs = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "raw value": model_data.loc[source_row, FEATURES],
        "standardized value": X_batch[OBSERVATION_POSITION],
    }
)
observation_inputs.index.name = "feature"

trace = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "hidden unit 1": [
            relu_outputs["hidden_scores"][OBSERVATION_POSITION, 0],
            relu_outputs["hidden_activations"][OBSERVATION_POSITION, 0],
        ],
        "hidden unit 2": [
            relu_outputs["hidden_scores"][OBSERVATION_POSITION, 1],
            relu_outputs["hidden_activations"][OBSERVATION_POSITION, 1],
        ],
        "hidden unit 3": [
            relu_outputs["hidden_scores"][OBSERVATION_POSITION, 2],
            relu_outputs["hidden_activations"][OBSERVATION_POSITION, 2],
        ],
    },
    index=["hidden score, Z[1]", "hidden activation, A[1]"],
)

print(f"Tracing source row {source_row}, whose observed label is {y_batch[OBSERVATION_POSITION]}.")
print("\nInputs used by this observation:")
display(observation_inputs.round(3))

title: Neural networks: forward propagation
text:
5. Why the activation function matters
A hidden layer without a nonlinear activation cannot create a more flexible function. If we replace ReLU with the identity function, the two linear layers collapse into one effective linear score before the final sigmoid.
We can verify that numerically.

identity_outputs = forward_pass(
    X=X_batch,
    weights_hidden=weights_hidden,
    bias_hidden=bias_hidden,
    weights_output=weights_output,
    bias_output=bias_output,
    activation=identity,
)

effective_weights = weights_output @ weights_hidden
effective_bias = bias_hidden @ weights_output.T + bias_output
collapsed_probabilities = sigmoid(
    X_batch @ effective_weights.T + effective_bias
)

np.testing.assert_allclose(
    actual=identity_outputs["probabilities"],
    desired=collapsed_probabilities,
)

activation_comparison = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "ReLU hidden layer": relu_outputs["probabilities"].ravel(),
        "identity hidden layer": identity_outputs["probabilities"].ravel(),
        "collapsed linear network": collapsed_probabilities.ravel(),
    },
    index=[f"source row {row}" for row in BATCH_ROWS],
)

print("The assertion passed: the identity network matches one linear score plus sigmoid.")

title: Neural networks: forward propagation
text:
6. Count the parameters
For \(p\) input features, \(h\) hidden units, and one output unit, this network has \(ph+h+h+1\) parameters: hidden weights and biases, then output weights and bias. Increasing hidden-layer width increases the model’s capacity and also increases the number of quantities that later need to be learned.

def count_parameters(*, n_features: int, n_hidden_units: int) -> int:
    """Count parameters in a one-hidden-layer binary classifier.

    Args:
        n_features: Number of input features.
        n_hidden_units: Number of hidden units.

    Returns:
        Total number of weights and biases in the network.
    """
    hidden_layer = n_features * n_hidden_units + n_hidden_units
    output_layer = n_hidden_units + 1
    return hidden_layer + output_layer

            count_parameters(n_features=9, n_hidden_units=4),

Takeaways

Forward propagation carries each observation through weighted sums and activation functions to produce a prediction.
With one row per observation, matrix shapes reveal how an entire batch can move through the network at once.
ReLU allows stacked hidden layers to avoid collapsing into one linear model.
The next question is how to choose the weights and biases from data. That requires a loss function and backpropagation.

title: How a decision tree grows
text:
This deliberately small two-feature example shows how a decision tree builds a piecewise decision boundary. Red triangles are positive observations (label 1) and green circles are negative observations (label 0). The animation follows a single greedy tree: each new rule is applied only to the observations that reached its parent node.






TipWhat to notice



The vertical rules do not extend over the entire feature space. They apply only inside the upper or lower region selected by an earlier rule on (x_2). A tree therefore creates a sequence of conditional decisions—not one global equation.

title: AdaBoost: learn from earlier mistakes
text:
A fully grown decision tree can fit a complicated set of rules, but it can also be sensitive to the particular observations it sees. AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting) takes a different route: it builds many decision stumps sequentially. A decision stump is a depth-1 tree with one split; we choose stumps here to make AdaBoost’s mechanics easy to see, not because deeper base trees are prohibited. Each later tree pays more attention to the training observations that the earlier trees found difficult.
We will use the same gas-turbine classification task as the decision-tree, bagging, and random-forest lessons. Each row records one operating observation; the target is a binary label.

title: AdaBoost: learn from earlier mistakes
text:
What you will do

Start with equal weight on every training observation and fit one depth-one tree, called a decision stump.
Increase the weights of observations that stump misclassifies.
Repeat the process to build a sequence of stumps, then pool their weighted votes.
Evaluate the intermediate boosted models on the same test set using AUC of ROC.

Unlike bagging and random forests, AdaBoost does not make bootstrap datasets. Every stump sees the same training rows; only their weights change.

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")

title: AdaBoost: learn from earlier mistakes
text:
1. Set up one training/test split
We keep one fixed split throughout the notebook. The test observations are never used to select a stump or update an observation weight.

FEATURES = ["AT", "AP", "AH", "AFDP", "GTEP", "TIT", "TAT", "TEY", "CDP"]
TARGET = "high_co"
RANDOM_STATE = 4520

data_candidates = [
    Path("../data/gas-turbine-course.csv"),
    Path("site/data/gas-turbine-course.csv"),
    Path("gas-turbine-course.csv"),
]
data_path = next((path for path in data_candidates if path.exists()), data_candidates[-1])
data = pd.read_csv(filepath_or_buffer=data_path)
model_data = data[FEATURES + [TARGET]].dropna().copy()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    model_data[FEATURES],
    model_data[TARGET],
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    stratify=model_data[TARGET],
)

print(f"Training observations: {len(X_train):,}")
print(f"Test observations: {len(X_test):,}")
print(f"Positive-label fraction in training data: {y_train.mean():.3f}")

title: AdaBoost: learn from earlier mistakes
text:
2. Fit the first weighted stump
At the first round, each training observation has the same weight, \(1/n\). A decision stump has just one split, so it is deliberately a weak individual model. AdaBoost will combine many of them.
For a stump \(h_t\), its weighted error is
\[
e_t = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i^{(t)}\,\mathbb{1}\!\left[h_t(\mathbf{x}_i) \ne y_i\right].
\]
The stump receives the vote weight
\[
\alpha_t = \frac{1}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{1-e_t}{e_t}\right).
\]
A lower weighted error gives a larger \(\alpha_t\), so a more reliable stump has more influence in the final vote.

def fit_adaboost_round(
    *,
    features: pd.DataFrame,
    labels: pd.Series,
    observation_weights: np.ndarray,
    random_state: int,
) -> tuple[DecisionTreeClassifier, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, float, float]:
    """Fit one AdaBoost stump and update the observation weights.

    Args:
        features: Training feature table.
        labels: Training binary labels.
        observation_weights: Normalized weights for the training observations.
        random_state: Seed used when fitting the decision stump.

    Returns:
        The fitted stump, its misclassified-training-sample mask, the normalized
        weights for the next round, its weighted error, and its vote weight.
    """
    stump = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=random_state)
    stump.fit(
        X=features,
        y=labels,
        sample_weight=observation_weights,
    )

    training_prediction = stump.predict(features).astype(int)
    incorrect = training_prediction != labels.to_numpy(dtype=int)
    weighted_error = float(observation_weights[incorrect].sum())
    alpha = 0.5 * np.log((1 - weighted_error) / weighted_error)

    multiplier = np.where(incorrect, np.exp(alpha), np.exp(-alpha))
    next_weights = observation_weights * multiplier
    next_weights = next_weights / next_weights.sum()

    return stump, incorrect, next_weights, weighted_error, float(alpha)


initial_weights = np.full(shape=len(X_train), fill_value=1 / len(X_train))
first_stump, first_incorrect, second_weights, first_error, first_alpha = fit_adaboost_round(
    features=X_train,
    labels=y_train,
    observation_weights=initial_weights,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
)

root_feature = FEATURES[first_stump.tree_.feature[0]]
root_threshold = first_stump.tree_.threshold[0]
print(f"First stump rule: {root_feature} ≤ {root_threshold:.3f}")
print(f"Weighted error: {first_error:.3f}")
print(f"Vote weight α₁: {first_alpha:.3f}")

First stump rule: TIT ≤ 1076.950
Weighted error: 0.154
Vote weight α₁: 0.852



What each fitted stump gives us
At boosting round \(t\), AdaBoost keeps track of a few different objects. The distinction between a single number and one value per training observation is important:









Object
Shape / constraint
Intuition
First-round example




Stump predictions \(h_t(\mathbf{x}_1), \ldots, h_t(\mathbf{x}_n)\)
Vector of length \(n\); entries are in \(\{0,1\}\)
They identify the samples the stump classifies correctly and those it misclassifies.
\(24{,}778\) predicted labels


Weighted error \(e_t\)
One scalar, \(0 \le e_t \le 1\)
The error made by the current stump, weighted by the current observation weights. Samples misclassified by earlier stumps tend to count more.
\(e_1 = 0.154\)


Vote weight \(\alpha_t\)
One scalar; positive when \(e_t < 0.5\)
How valuable this base model is to the ensemble: a more reliable stump receives a larger vote in the final prediction.
\(\alpha_1 = 0.852\)


Current observation weights \(\mathbf{w}^{(t)}\)
Vector of length \(n\); each entry is nonnegative and the entries sum to \(1\)
One importance value per training observation; these weights are used to fit the current stump.
Initially, every entry is \(1/24{,}778 \approx 0.0000404\)


Updated observation weights \(\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)}\)
Vector of length \(n\); each entry is nonnegative and the entries sum to \(1\)
After we increase the weights of misclassified samples and normalize, this vector tells the next stump where to focus.
Misclassified samples: \(0.000131\) each; correctly classified samples: \(0.0000239\) each



Let’s now construct that updated weight vector.

title: AdaBoost: learn from earlier mistakes
section: 3. Increase the weight of misclassified samples
text:
3. Increase the weight of misclassified samples
After fitting stump \(t\), its misclassified samples should matter more to the next stump. The key idea of AdaBoost’s update is to rebalance attention: after reweighting, the samples misclassified by the current stump collectively carry half of the total weight, and the samples it classified correctly carry the other half.
Before the update, those two groups carry total weights \(e_t\) and \(1-e_t\), respectively. The \(\alpha_t\) selected in Section 2 satisfies
\[
e_t\exp(\alpha_t) = (1-e_t)\exp(-\alpha_t),
\]
so multiplying the misclassified and correctly classified samples by the following factors gives both groups the same total weight before normalization. After normalization, each group has weight \(0.5\). The two groups are defined by the current stump, so they can change at the next round.
We keep the labels and stump predictions as \(y_i, h_t(\mathbf{x}_i) \in \{0,1\}\). First, create one multiplier for each training observation:
\[
m_i^{(t)} = \exp(\alpha_t) \qquad \text{if } h_t(\mathbf{x}_i) \ne y_i.
\]
\[
m_i^{(t)} = \exp(-\alpha_t) \qquad \text{if } h_t(\mathbf{x}_i) = y_i.
\]
Then multiply the current weight by that multiplier and renormalize all weights to sum to one:
\[
w_i^{(t+1)} = \frac{w_i^{(t)}m_i^{(t)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j^{(t)}m_j^{(t)}}.
\]
This is exactly what the code does with np.where(...): a mistake receives \(\exp(\alpha_t)\), a correct prediction receives \(\exp(-\alpha_t)\), and the final division by the sum normalizes the new weights.
For the first stump, the following table compares the total training weight carried by correctly classified and misclassified samples.

weight_shift = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Before the update": [
            initial_weights[~first_incorrect].sum(),
            initial_weights[first_incorrect].sum(),
        ],
        "After the update": [
            second_weights[~first_incorrect].sum(),
            second_weights[first_incorrect].sum(),
        ],
    },
    index=["Correctly classified samples", "Misclassified samples"],
)

The first stump misclassified only a fraction of the training samples, but after the update those same samples carry half of the total weight. The next stump is therefore pushed toward a complementary rule.

title: AdaBoost: learn from earlier mistakes
text:
4. Repeat the weighted fitting process
Now let’s repeat Sections 2 and 3 for twelve rounds. At every round, we fit a stump using the current observation weights, compute its weighted error and vote weight, then update the weights for the next stump. The fitted stumps and their vote weights together form the trained AdaBoost model.
We calculate held-out AUC after each round only to inspect how the progressively larger ensemble performs.

def fit_adaboost(
    *,
    training_features: pd.DataFrame,
    training_labels: pd.Series,
    test_features: pd.DataFrame,
    test_labels: pd.Series,
    n_rounds: int,
    random_state: int,
) -> tuple[list[DecisionTreeClassifier], pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]:
    """Fit sequential AdaBoost stumps and record held-out AUC.

    Args:
        training_features: Feature table used to fit every stump.
        training_labels: Binary labels for the training observations.
        test_features: Held-out feature table used only for evaluation.
        test_labels: Held-out binary labels.
        n_rounds: Number of sequential stumps to fit.
        random_state: Seed for reproducible stump fitting.

    Returns:
        The fitted stumps, a round-by-round summary, and test-set scores
        from the final weighted ensemble.
    """
    weights = np.full(shape=len(training_features), fill_value=1 / len(training_features))
    ensemble_margin = np.zeros(shape=len(test_features))
    alpha_total = 0.0
    stumps = []
    records = []

    for round_index in range(n_rounds):
        stump, incorrect, weights, weighted_error, alpha = fit_adaboost_round(
            features=training_features,
            labels=training_labels,
            observation_weights=weights,
            random_state=random_state,
        )
        test_prediction = stump.predict(test_features).astype(int)
        ensemble_margin += alpha * (2 * test_prediction - 1)
        alpha_total += alpha
        positive_vote = (ensemble_margin / alpha_total + 1) / 2

        stumps.append(stump)
        records.append(
            {
                "Round": round_index + 1,
                "Feature": FEATURES[stump.tree_.feature[0]],
                "Weighted error": weighted_error,
                "Vote weight α": alpha,
                "Held-out AUC": roc_auc_score(test_labels, positive_vote),
            }
        )

    return stumps, pd.DataFrame(records), positive_vote


stumps, round_summary, final_test_score = fit_adaboost(
    training_features=X_train,
    training_labels=y_train,
    test_features=X_test,
    test_labels=y_test,
    n_rounds=12,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
)

text:
5. Use the trained model for prediction
For a new feature vector \(\mathbf{x}\), each trained stump votes for label 0 or 1. The ensemble combines those votes using the \(\alpha_t\) values rather than giving every stump the same influence:
\[
s_T(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t h_t(\mathbf{x})}{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t}.
\]
This score ranks observations from more negative-like to more positive-like. It is useful for AUC of ROC, but unlike a logistic-regression output, it is not automatically a calibrated probability. Let’s inspect the weighted vote for one held-out operating observation.

title: AdaBoost: learn from earlier mistakes
text:
6. What AdaBoost changes

Bagging / random forests: independent trees are averaged. Their diversity comes from bootstrap samples and, for random forests, random feature candidates.
AdaBoost: trees are fitted one after another. Their diversity comes from repeatedly changing which training observations receive the most weight.
The main hyperparameters here are the number of stumps, their depth, and a learning rate that can shrink each stump’s vote weight.
AdaBoost’s emphasis on hard cases can be useful, but it can also make the model sensitive to mislabeled observations or outliers. Gradient boosting will keep the sequential idea while generalizing it to directly reduce a chosen loss function.

Open the AdaBoost explorer
Return to Tree-based models

title: Bagging: many bootstrap-trained trees
text:
A decision tree can be very sensitive to the particular observations it is trained on, i.e., overfit (high-variance). Bagging (bootstrap aggregating), which is one type of ensemble methods, can help to reduce the variance. Specifically, we fit many trees on bootstrap versions of one training dataset, then average their predictions.
We will use the gas-turbine positive-label task to see each part of that process.

title: Bagging: many bootstrap-trained trees
text:
What you will do

Construct bootstrap datasets mechanically: sample the training rows with replacement.
Fit one deep tree on this dataset and evaluate it on held-out observations.
Repeat steps 1 and 2 to obtain multiple models (trees), then make a prediction by averaging each base model’s prediction.
Compare individual bootstrap trees and the bagged ensemble on the same test set.


from pathlib import Path

2. Make one bootstrap dataset
A bootstrap dataset has exactly \(n\) rows when the original training set has \(n\) rows. We draw the rows with replacement, so a source row can be used zero, one, or several times. The total number of draws remains \(n\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=RANDOM_STATE)
bootstrap_positions = rng.integers(low=0, high=len(X_train), size=len(X_train))
bootstrap_counts = np.bincount(bootstrap_positions, minlength=len(X_train))
X_bootstrap = X_train.iloc[bootstrap_positions].reset_index(drop=True)
y_bootstrap = y_train.iloc[bootstrap_positions].reset_index(drop=True)

bootstrap_overview = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "number of appearances": [0, 1, 2, 3, "4+"],
        "training rows": [
            np.sum(bootstrap_counts == 0),
            np.sum(bootstrap_counts == 1),
            np.sum(bootstrap_counts == 2),
            np.sum(bootstrap_counts == 3),
            np.sum(bootstrap_counts >= 4),
        ],
    }
)
print(f"Bootstrap draws: {len(bootstrap_positions):,}")
print(f"Distinct source rows represented: {np.sum(bootstrap_counts > 0):,}")

title: Bagging: many bootstrap-trained trees
section: 3. Fit one tree to that dataset
text:
3. Fit one tree to that dataset
We fit one depth-5 decision tree to the bootstrap dataset. ROC AUC measures how well its probability scores rank positive and negative observations in the held-out test set.

def auc_scores(
    *,
    model: Any,
    X_train: pd.DataFrame,
    y_train: pd.Series,
    X_test: pd.DataFrame,
    y_test: pd.Series,
) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Compute training and held-out ROC AUC for a fitted classifier.

    Args:
        model: A fitted classifier that provides ``predict_proba``.
        X_train: Features used to fit the model.
        y_train: Training labels.
        X_test: Held-out feature values.
        y_test: Held-out labels.

    Returns:
        Training and held-out ROC AUC values.
    """
    training_probability = model.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]
    test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    return {
        "training AUC": roc_auc_score(y_train, training_probability),
        "test AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability),
    }


one_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=MAX_DEPTH, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
one_tree.fit(X=X_bootstrap, y=y_bootstrap)
one_tree_scores = auc_scores(
    model=one_tree,
    X_train=X_bootstrap,
    y_train=y_bootstrap,
    X_test=X_test,
    y_test=y_test,
)
pd.DataFrame([one_tree_scores], index=[f"One depth-{MAX_DEPTH} bootstrap tree"]).round(3)

title: Bagging: many bootstrap-trained trees
section: 4. Repeat the process and pool the predictions
text:
4. Repeat the process and pool the predictions
Bagging repeats steps 2 and 3 \(B\) times. Each tree is fitted independently on one bootstrap dataset. For a new feature vector \(\mathbf{x}\), the ensemble averages the trees’ positive-label probabilities:
\[
\hat{p}_{\mathrm{bag}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \hat{p}_{b}(\mathbf{x}).
\]

N_TREES = 200

bagging = BaggingClassifier(
    estimator=DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=MAX_DEPTH),
    n_estimators=N_TREES,
    bootstrap=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
)
bagging.fit(X=X_train, y=y_train)

bagging_scores = auc_scores(
    model=bagging,
    X_train=X_train,
    y_train=y_train,
    X_test=X_test,
    y_test=y_test,
)
pd.DataFrame(
    [one_tree_scores, bagging_scores],
    index=[f"One depth-{MAX_DEPTH} bootstrap tree", f"Bagging ({N_TREES} trees)"],
).round(3)

title: Bagging: many bootstrap-trained trees
section: 5. Pool the tree predictions for one held-out observation
text:
5. Pool the tree predictions for one held-out observation
For one fixed held-out observation, each fitted tree produces a probability. Bagging uses their running average as its pooled prediction.

def individual_tree_probabilities(*, model: Any, X: pd.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    """Collect held-out positive-label probabilities from every bagged tree.

    Args:
        model: A fitted bagging classifier.
        X: Feature values to score.

    Returns:
        An array with one probability column per fitted tree.
    """
    X_values = X.to_numpy()
    return np.column_stack(
        [tree.predict_proba(X_values)[:, 1] for tree in model.estimators_]
    )


bagging_tree_probabilities = individual_tree_probabilities(model=bagging, X=X_test)
tree_counts = np.arange(1, N_TREES + 1)
example_label = int(y_test.iloc[FIXED_TEST_POSITION])
example_probabilities = bagging_tree_probabilities[FIXED_TEST_POSITION]
running_probability = np.cumsum(example_probabilities) / tree_counts

print(f"Fixed observation label: {example_label}")
print(f"Pooled probability after {N_TREES} trees: {running_probability[-1]:.3f}")

fig, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.4))
axis.scatter(
    tree_counts,
    example_probabilities,
    color=bagging_color,
    alpha=0.28,
    s=20,
    label="Individual tree probability",
)
axis.plot(
    tree_counts,
    running_probability,
    color=bagging_color,
    linewidth=2.5,
    label="Pooled average",
)
axis.set(
    title="Bagging pools the probabilities from individual trees",
    xlabel="Tree added to the ensemble",
    ylabel="Predicted positive-label probability",
    xlim=(1, N_TREES),
    ylim=(-0.06, 1.06),
)
axis.legend(loc="center right")
sns.despine(ax=axis)
plt.show()

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
text:
The data we are dealing with in practice are a finite sample from a larger – most likely infinite – population of possible observations. That population may be a physical process operating over time, manufactured parts produced under the same conditions, or outcomes that could have occurred under comparable conditions. We use the sample to infer properties of the population.
That inference comes with uncertainty because a different sampling trial could have produced a different result (e.g., a different collection of observations). Null hypothesis testing gives us a disciplined way to ask whether an observed result is surprising under a reference claim about the population.
Learning objectives

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
text:
1. An engineering question
Suppose a machining process is intended to produce shafts with a diameter of 20.00 mm. Due to the inevitable variability during the manufacturing process, the diameters of the shafts produced will vary. However, we would assume the distribution of diameters is centered at 20.00 mm, i.e., the population mean is 20.00 mm. A quality engineer samples 25 shafts and obtains a sample mean of 20.20 mm, with the sample standard deviation of 0.40 mm.
The sample mean is above the target, but seemingly close to it. Is a difference of 0.20 mm evidence that the process (i.e., population) mean is different from 20.00 mm, or could it plausibly be ordinary sampling variation?

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
section: 2. From observations to a population claim
text:
2. From observations to a population claim
The 25 measured shafts are our sample. The quantity we want to learn about is the process’s long-run mean diameter across the much larger population of shafts it could produce. We cannot measure that entire population, so we use the sample mean to infer its mean.
The observed mean is 0.20 mm above the target. There are two broad explanations: ordinary sampling variation from a process still centered at 20.00 mm, or evidence that the process mean is genuinely different. Null hypothesis testing makes that comparison precise by asking how surprising this sample would be under the first explanation.

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
text:
3. State the competing hypotheses
Let \(\mu\) be the true, long-run mean shaft diameter for this process. The null hypothesis is the reference claim we want to examine:
\[H_0: \mu = 20.00\text{ mm}\]
The alternative hypothesis describes the kind of departure we care about:
\[H_A: \mu \ne 20.00\text{ mm}\]
This is a two-sided test because a mean that is too small or too large would both be evidence against the target. The hypotheses are statements about the population mean, not about the particular sample we happened to measure.

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
text:
4. Simulate the null world
To assess the observed mean, imagine repeatedly taking new samples of 25 shafts in a world where \(H_0\) is true. For this simulation, we make a deliberate shortcut: we use the observed sample standard deviation, \(S = 0.40\) mm, as if it were the population standard deviation, \(\sigma\).
We also assume that individual shaft diameters follow a normal distribution centered at 20.00 mm. We start with a Normal population because it makes the result especially clean: the mean of 25 such shafts is exactly Normally distributed. This is not a requirement for using a Normal-shaped null distribution of sample means. The central limit theorem (CLT) explains why a similar pattern can arise even when the individual diameters are not Normal.
For each repetition, we draw 25 individual diameters and calculate their sample mean. Repeating that process produces a null distribution: the values of the test statistic (here, the sample mean) that would arise if the process had not shifted. According to CLT, the null distribution is a Normal distribution, centered at 20.00 mm, with standard error \(0.40 / \sqrt{25} = 0.08\) mm.

# NumPy simulates repeated samples; Matplotlib displays their distributions.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
rng = np.random.default_rng(4520)

target_mean = 20.00  # mm: the null population mean
observed_mean = 20.20  # mm: the measured sample mean
sample_sd = 0.40  # mm: the measured sample standard deviation
sample_size = 25

# Teaching shortcut: use the sample SD as the population SD in this simulation.
population_sd = sample_sd
standard_error = population_sd / np.sqrt(sample_size)

n_repetitions = 100_000
# Each row is one hypothetical quality sample of 25 normally distributed shafts
# from a process whose population mean is still the target mean.
normal_null_samples = rng.normal(
    loc=target_mean,
    scale=population_sd,
    size=(n_repetitions, sample_size),
)
null_means = normal_null_samples.mean(axis=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.hist(null_means, bins=60, density=True, color="#4a90c2", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(target_mean, color="#355766", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="Null mean: 20.00 mm")
ax.axvline(observed_mean, color="#b65420", linewidth=2.5, label="Observed mean: 20.20 mm")
ax.set(
    xlabel="Sample mean diameter (mm)",
    ylabel="Density across repeated samples",
    title="Null distribution of sample means: normally distributed shaft diameters",
)
ax.legend(frameon=True)
plt.show()

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
text:
5. Calculate and interpret a p-value
The observed mean is 0.20 mm from the null mean. For a two-sided test, we count simulated means at least that far away in either direction. The resulting proportion is the p-value.
\[p\text{-value} = P\left(\left|\bar{X} - 20.00\right| \geq \left|20.20 - 20.00\right| \;\middle|\; H_0\right)\]
Read the vertical bar as assuming the null hypothesis is true. A p-value is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true. It is the probability of seeing a result at least this unusual if \(H_0\) were true.

observed_distance = abs(observed_mean - target_mean)
as_extreme = abs(null_means - target_mean) >= observed_distance
p_value = as_extreme.mean()

bin_edges = np.linspace(null_means.min(), null_means.max(), 61)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.hist(null_means, bins=bin_edges, color="#d6e6f1", edgecolor="white")
ax.hist(
    null_means[as_extreme], bins=bin_edges,
    color="#d77732", edgecolor="white", label="At least as extreme under $H_0$"
)
ax.axvline(target_mean, color="#355766", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
ax.axvline(observed_mean, color="#b65420", linewidth=2.5, label="Observed mean")
ax.axvline(2 * target_mean - observed_mean, color="#b65420", linewidth=2.5)
ax.set(
    xlabel="Sample mean diameter (mm)",
    ylabel="Number of simulated samples",
    title=f"Two-sided simulated p-value: {p_value:.3f}",
)
ax.legend(frameon=True)
plt.show()

print(f"Observed distance from the target: {observed_distance:.2f} mm")
print(f"Estimated two-sided p-value: {p_value:.3f}")








Observed distance from the target: 0.20 mm
Estimated two-sided p-value: 0.013

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
text:
6. Turn evidence into a decision
The p-value tells us how surprising the observed mean would be under the first explanation, i.e., Null hypothesis \(H_0\): ordinary sampling variation from a process still centered at 20.00 mm. To turn that evidence into a principled decision framework, we need to choose a decision threshold (for the p-value) before seeing the data.
This threshold is called the significance level, \(\alpha\). A commonly used value is \(\alpha = 0.05\). With this choice, we reject \(H_0\) when the p-value is below 0.05; otherwise, we fail to reject \(H_0\). The choice of \(\alpha\) should reflect the consequence of falsely declaring that the process has shifted. If \(H_0\) is actually true, a rule with \(\alpha = 0.05\) makes a Type-I error—a false rejection—about 5% of the time in the long run.
The rejection region is the set of sample-mean values for which our testing procedure rejects \(H_0\). Before seeing the sample outcome, we choose the test to be two-sided, choose \(\alpha\), and specify the reference distribution. The numerical boundaries can still depend on an estimated quantity. Here, because the population standard deviation is unknown, we plug the observed \(S = 0.40\) mm into \(\sigma\) to calculate them.
In a two-sided test with \(\alpha = 0.05\), the intended rejection region contains the outer 5% of the null distribution: 2.5% in each tail. Under the null model, this gives a Type-I error rate of about 5% in the long run.
For this Normal/CLT reference calculation, the two-sided 5% rule uses 1.96 standard errors from the target:
\[
\bar{X} < 20.00 - 1.96(0.08) = 19.843\text{ mm}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\bar{X} > 20.00 + 1.96(0.08) = 20.157\text{ mm}.
\]
The shaded tails below are the plug-in rejection region for \(S = 0.40\) mm. The testing procedure is pre-specified; after obtaining \(S\), we calculate its numerical boundaries and check whether \(\bar{X}=20.20\) mm falls inside them.

alpha = 0.05
z_critical = 1.96
critical_distance = z_critical * standard_error
lower_cutoff = target_mean - critical_distance
upper_cutoff = target_mean + critical_distance
type_i_error_rate = np.mean(
    (null_means <= lower_cutoff) | (null_means >= upper_cutoff)
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.hist(null_means, bins=60, density=True, color="#d6e6f1", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvspan(null_means.min(), lower_cutoff, color="#d77732", alpha=0.45, label="Reject $H_0$")
ax.axvspan(upper_cutoff, null_means.max(), color="#d77732", alpha=0.45)
ax.axvline(observed_mean, color="#b65420", linewidth=2.5, label="Observed mean")
ax.set(
    xlabel="Sample mean diameter (mm)",
    ylabel="Density across repeated samples",
    title="A 5% two-sided decision rule under the null hypothesis",
)
ax.legend(frameon=True)
plt.show()

print(f"Reject H₀ below {lower_cutoff:.3f} mm or above {upper_cutoff:.3f} mm.")
print(f"Simulated Type-I error rate: {type_i_error_rate:.3f}")
print("Decision for this sample:", "reject H₀" if p_value < alpha else "fail to reject H₀")








Reject H₀ below 19.843 mm or above 20.157 mm.
Simulated Type-I error rate: 0.051
Decision for this sample: reject H₀



Decision at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The simulated p-value is about 0.013, below the pre-specified 5% threshold. We therefore reject \(H_0\): under this null model, the data provide evidence against the explanation that the process is still centered at 20.00 mm. This decision does not prove that the process mean has shifted.


Try it
Keep the observed difference at 0.20 mm, but change the sample size. What happens to the standard error and to the simulated p-value when you use 9, 25, or 100 shafts?

title: Null hypothesis testing: evidence and decisions
section: 7. What statistical significance does—and does not—say
text:
7. What statistical significance does—and does not—say
A small p-value is evidence that the observed result would be unusual under the null model. It does not tell us:

the probability that the null hypothesis is true;
whether a detected shift is large enough to matter for engineering tolerances;
whether one variable causes another to change.

A larger sample can make a very small deviation statistically significant. Always report an estimated effect and its confidence interval alongside a p-value, then use engineering judgment to decide whether the effect matters.
In the Regression series, we will apply the same logic to a slope. There, the null hypothesis will be \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\): no linear association between a predictor and the response in the model.

text:

title: Probability distributions and simulation
text:
Engineers use probability distributions to describe quantities that vary: a manufacturing dimension, a load, a sensor reading, or an emission measurement. In this notebook, you will use NumPy to simulate and visualize a few common distributions.
This is preparation for our in-class discussion of the central limit theorem (CLT). We will discuss sampling distributions, formal hypothesis tests, and p-values together in class.
Learning objectives

title: Probability distributions and simulation
text:
1. Set up a simulation
A simulation creates artificial observations according to rules we specify. This lets us isolate one statistical idea at a time before working with messier engineering measurements.

# NumPy generates random samples; Matplotlib displays them.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
# A fixed seed makes the examples reproducible: everyone sees the same draw.
rng = np.random.default_rng(4520)

title: Probability distributions and simulation
text:
2. Draw samples from probability distributions
A distribution describes the values a variable can take and how frequently different values occur. We will begin with three useful distribution shapes. These are useful approximations, not automatic labels for every engineering variable: choosing a distribution should be guided by the physical mechanism and by observed data.

Normal distribution
A normal distribution is symmetric around a typical value and is often useful when many small, independent sources of variation add together. A familiar example is adult height within a relatively homogeneous population. An engineering example is repeated measurements of a machined part’s diameter when the process is stable.
rng.normal(loc, scale, size) draws size observations with mean loc and standard deviation scale.

# Simulate 1,000 measurements centered at 50 with a spread of 8.
normal_sample = rng.normal(loc=50, scale=8, size=1_000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.hist(normal_sample, bins=30, color="#4a90c2", edgecolor="white")
ax.set(
    xlabel="Simulated measurement",
    ylabel="Number of observations",
    title="A simulated normal distribution",
)
plt.show()

print(f"Sample mean: {normal_sample.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Sample standard deviation: {normal_sample.std(ddof=1):.2f}")








Sample mean: 49.76
Sample standard deviation: 7.84




Try it
Draw a normal sample centered at 100 with a standard deviation of 15. How do its histogram and sample summary differ from the one above?

# my_sample = rng.normal(loc=..., scale=..., size=...)
# print(my_sample.mean())
# print(my_sample.std(ddof=1))



Uniform distribution
In a uniform distribution, every value in an interval is equally likely. A familiar example is an ideal random-number generator that returns any number from 0 to 1. An engineering simulation might choose an initial shaft angle at random between two limits, or sample evenly across an allowable tolerance range.
rng.uniform(low, high, size) draws values evenly between two limits. Unlike the normal distribution, it has no single central value that is more likely than another within that interval.

# Draw 5,000 values with equal probability anywhere from 0 to 10.
uniform = rng.uniform(low=0, high=10, size=5_000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.hist(uniform, bins=35, density=True, color="#77a464", edgecolor="white")
ax.set(title="A simulated uniform distribution", xlabel="Value", ylabel="Density")
plt.show()










Exponential distribution
An exponential distribution is nonnegative and right-skewed, so it is often used to model waiting times. A familiar example is the waiting time until the next customer arrives when arrivals occur independently at a roughly constant average rate. In engineering, it can model the lifetime of one component when its instantaneous failure rate is assumed constant: a component that has already operated for 10 hours is, under this simplified model, no more or less likely to fail in the next hour than a new one.
rng.exponential(scale, size) draws nonnegative, right-skewed values. Its average is approximately scale; most draws are relatively small, but occasionally a much larger value occurs.

# Draw 5,000 waiting times with an average value of 2.
exponential = rng.exponential(scale=2, size=5_000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.hist(exponential, bins=35, density=True, color="#d9903d", edgecolor="white")
ax.set(title="A simulated exponential distribution", xlabel="Value", ylabel="Density")
plt.show()

title: Type-I and Type-II errors: decisions under uncertainty
text: A hypothesis test makes a decision from limited observations. The population state is not directly observable, so even a well-designed decision rule can make mistakes. This page develops the general structure of those mistakes before returning to the shaft-diameter example.

title: Type-I and Type-II errors: decisions under uncertainty
text:
Learning objectives

Distinguish the actual state of the world from a test decision.
Locate Type-I and Type-II errors in a general \(2\times2\) table.
Recognize the same structure in judicial and medical settings.

title: Type-I and Type-II errors: decisions under uncertainty
section: 1. Decisions and truth are different things
text:
1. Decisions and truth are different things
A hypothesis test has two possible decisions: reject \(H_0\) or fail to reject \(H_0\). Meanwhile, the population has one of two possible states: \(H_0\) is true or \(H_0\) is false. In this two-sided test, a false \(H_0\) corresponds to \(H_A\) being true. The test decision is based on a sample; the population state is the underlying reality that generated it.
In one particular application, we usually do not get to observe that reality with certainty. The \(2\times2\) table instead describes what happens across many comparable decisions.
One wording matters: fail to reject \(H_0\) does not mean accept \(H_0\). It means that the observed sample did not provide sufficient evidence against \(H_0\) under the chosen decision rule.

title: Type-I and Type-II errors: decisions under uncertainty
text:
2. The general \(2\times2\) table








Actual population state
Fail to reject \(H_0\)
Reject \(H_0\)




\(H_0\) is true
Correct decision
Type-I error: reject a true null hypothesis


\(H_A\) is true
Type-II error: fail to reject a false null hypothesis
Correct detection



A Type-I error is a false positive: the procedure signals a difference when no difference is actually present. A Type-II error is a false negative: the procedure misses a difference that is actually present.

title: Type-I and Type-II errors: decisions under uncertainty
section: 3. The same structure in familiar settings
text:
3. The same structure in familiar settings
The terminology becomes clearer when we identify the null hypothesis, the action represented by rejecting it, and the four possible outcomes.

Judicial setting
Take the null hypothesis, \(H_0\), to be: the defendant is innocent. Rejecting \(H_0\) corresponds to conviction.








Actual state
Do not convict (fail to reject \(H_0\))
Convict (reject \(H_0\))




Defendant is innocent
Correct: do not convict
Type-I error: convict an innocent person


Defendant is guilty
Type-II error: fail to convict a guilty person
Correct conviction



The language of not guilty parallels fail to reject: it is not a claim that the defendant is known to be innocent.


Medical screening
For a screening test, take \(H_0\) to be: the patient does not have the disease. Rejecting \(H_0\) corresponds to a positive screen.








Actual state
Negative screen (fail to reject \(H_0\))
Positive screen (reject \(H_0\))




Patient does not have the disease
Correct negative
Type-I error: false positive


Patient has the disease
Type-II error: false negative
Correct positive



Which error is more serious depends on the condition, the follow-up test, and the consequences of delayed treatment.


Shaft-diameter process
Return now to our machining process. Take \(H_0\) to be: the process mean shaft diameter is 20.00 mm. Rejecting \(H_0\) means investigating or adjusting the process.








Actual process state
Continue operation (fail to reject \(H_0\))
Investigate or adjust (reject \(H_0\))




Process is centered at 20.00 mm
Correct: leave a stable process alone
Type-I error: unnecessarily interrupt a stable process


Process mean has shifted
Type-II error: miss a real shift
Correct detection: investigate or adjust the process

title: Type-I and Type-II errors: decisions under uncertainty
section: 4. From error types to error rates
text:
4. From error types to error rates
The \(2\times2\) table names the possible outcomes of one decision. To design a test, we also need to describe how often its errors occur over many comparable samples.

Type-I error rate: \(\alpha\)
The significance level, \(\alpha\), is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis:
\[
\alpha = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true}).
\]
We choose \(\alpha\) before examining the data. With \(\alpha = 0.05\), a decision procedure is designed to make a Type-I error about 5% of the time when \(H_0\) is true.


Type-II error rate: \(\beta\)
The Type-II error rate is the probability of failing to reject \(H_0\) when a particular alternative is actually true:
\[
\beta(\mu_A) = P(\text{fail to reject } H_0 \mid \mu = \mu_A).
\]
Unlike \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) is not one universal number. It depends on which real shift we are trying to detect. For the shaft process, missing a shift to \(20.05\) mm is more likely than missing a shift to \(20.30\) mm.
The probability of correctly rejecting \(H_0\) when that particular alternative is true is the power of the test:
\[
\text{power}(\mu_A) = 1 - \beta(\mu_A).
\]

title: A first look at gas-turbine emissions data
text:
4. Ask a distribution question
Our question is: how common are high-NOx operating hours? A histogram shows how frequently a range of values occurs. If the distribution is not symmetric, reporting only a mean can hide useful information about high-emission observations.

# Compare the mean and median to see whether a single center summarizes NOx well.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.hist(data["NOX"], bins=50, color="#4a90c2", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(data["NOX"].mean(), color="#c43c35", linestyle="--", label="mean")
ax.axvline(data["NOX"].median(), color="#222222", linestyle=":", label="median")
ax.set(xlabel="NOx emissions (mg/m³)", ylabel="Number of hourly observations", title="Distribution of NOx emissions")
ax.legend()
plt.show()









A compact view: boxplot
A boxplot compresses the same distribution into a few robust summaries. The line inside the box is the median, and the box spans the middle 50% of observations (the interquartile range, IQR). By the usual 1.5 × IQR convention used here, each whisker reaches the most extreme observed value still within 1.5 IQR below the first quartile or above the third quartile; points beyond the whiskers are potential outliers. Boxplots are especially useful when comparing distributions across variables or operating groups later in the course.

# A horizontal boxplot makes the center, spread, and unusually high NOx values easy to compare.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.5))
ax.boxplot(
    data["NOX"],
    vert=False,
    patch_artist=True,
    boxprops={"facecolor": "#4a90c2", "alpha": 0.7},
)
ax.set(xlabel="NOx emissions (mg/m³)", title="Boxplot of NOx emissions")
plt.show()

title: A first look at gas-turbine emissions data
text:
5. Screen for associations
Now ask: which measurements move together strongly enough to investigate? A correlation heatmap is a compact screen for linear associations. It helps us choose questions and plots; it does not establish a causal mechanism, because sensors can respond to the same operating state.

# Correlations describe linear association; they do not establish a causal mechanism.
correlations = data[key_variables].corr(numeric_only=True)

# A shared color scale makes strong positive and negative associations easy to spot.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
heatmap = ax.imshow(correlations, cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
# Disable the notebook-wide white grid so it does not draw over the heatmap cells.
ax.grid(False)

ax.set_xticks(range(len(key_variables)), key_variables, rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(key_variables)), key_variables)
ax.set_title("Correlation heatmap for selected gas-turbine variables")

# Label each cell so the heatmap remains useful when printed or viewed in grayscale.
for row in range(len(key_variables)):
    for column in range(len(key_variables)):
        value = correlations.iloc[row, column]
        text_color = "white" if abs(value) > 0.5 else "black"
        ax.text(column, row, f"{value:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", color=text_color)

fig.colorbar(heatmap, ax=ax, label="Pearson correlation")
plt.show()









# Use a fixed random subset to keep the scatter plots legible and reproducible.
plot_data = data.sample(n=3_000, random_state=4520)

# Inspect two candidate associations visually before drawing conclusions from a correlation value.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), constrained_layout=True)
axes[0].scatter(plot_data["TIT"], plot_data["NOX"], alpha=0.2, s=10)
axes[0].set(xlabel="Turbine inlet temperature, TIT (°C)", ylabel="NOx (mg/m³)", title="Temperature and NOx")

axes[1].scatter(plot_data["TEY"], plot_data["CO"], alpha=0.2, s=10, color="#c43c35")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Turbine energy yield, TEY (MWh)", ylabel="CO (mg/m³)", title="Energy yield and CO")

plt.show()
